# Glossary for The History of the Kings of Britain

**Read in:** [UK English](uk/GLOSSARY.md)

The people, places and words of Geoffrey of Monmouth's *History of the Kings of Britain*.

[^ryan-allen]: **Ryan Allen** designs and builds software. Good work disappears into what it's for. [ryanallen.com](https://ryanallen.com) · [GitHub](https://github.com/ryanallen) · [LinkedIn](https://www.linkedin.com/in/ryanallencom) · [Leaftext](https://leaftext.com)

[^how-designed-the-system]: The tools that made this book, its checks and the rules they hold were designed as one system, and every line in it came out of that system. When a passage reads wrong, the fix goes into the system and the book is made again, never written in by hand, so it reaches every book on the shelf.

[^how-all-checks-passed]: Every range was run through the book's own check tool and the shelf's checks, and nothing was ticked done until they passed: a missing page, a broken link, an old word, a word repeated too soon, a wrong mark and a change nobody logged are all refused.

[^how-readable-first]: Each passage is told the way a good English writer would tell it today, then checked against the source so every event, person and act is there and nothing is invented.

[^how-plain-speech]: No Bible cadence and no stiff old-translation voice: no chains of "and… and… and", no solemn word order, no word nobody says now.

[^how-shaped-for-english]: Each sentence is written as English, not in the source's grammar: a verb rather than a noun made of one, never a clause hanging off a clause, and what someone must do before where or why, with nothing lost. Every sentence that says a common verb twice was read and either rewritten or kept with the reason.

[^how-every-link-said]: Where the source joins a cause and its effect with a bare "and", the English says how they connect, with "to", "by", "so", "until" or "because"; where it strings quotations together, the English says who speaks each one and why, never a bare "Again:".

[^how-nothing-said-twice]: What the source says twice, a doubled verb or a speech the narration has just told, is said once, unless a speaker repeats it on purpose, and the book's account of its text is given once, its edition and scans cited in full only under Sources.

[^how-the-right-word-each-time]: A source word with several senses takes the English its moment needs, never one word everywhere and never the vaguest.

[^how-no-word-worn-out]: No word comes back within forty words of itself, names and the commonest grammar words aside; the second use takes another word or goes.

[^how-modern-idiom]: Old English turns give way to the ones people use now, in how people talk to and about each other as much as in rare words: "pregnant", "said goodbye", "my mom". Every word judged old is kept in the shelf's list, and the check refuses each one.

[^how-us-english]: The reviewed US master uses Merriam-Webster spelling and usage, the article a US reader says, as "an herb", *The Chicago Manual of Style*, and lengths and distances in feet and miles. A later UK edition is made from that master.

[^how-natural-tenses]: The story is told in the simple past wherever the order of events is plain, as English tells it, not in the source's stacked past tenses.

[^how-neutral-tone]: No archaism and no color the source doesn't give, but a hard word stays hard.

[^how-gender-neutral]: Where the source means anyone, the English says "they", "people" or "anyone", never "he" and never a pair of pronouns; a figure the source names keeps the pronoun the source gives.

[^how-no-false-echoes]: No English turn that calls up a better-known story the source doesn't mean: Christ leads Adam and Eve out of hell, never "casts them out", which calls up Eden. An echo the source means stays.

[^how-read-aloud]: Every sentence or line was read aloud and its slack cut with no fact dropped; prose stays in paragraphs, and verse keeps its lines and stanzas, and its beat and rhyme wherever they survive.

[^how-scenes-read-for-movement]: Each whole scene was read for what each speaker wants and where it turns, and the whole book in order, so the dialogue and paragraph breaks carry it; nothing the source doesn't give was added.

[^how-sources-named]: Every reading says whose it is: the scholars who edited the text by name, the printing by its year, the handwritten copy by its own name, and this translation's own work as "this translation", never "we".

[^how-honest-where-unsure]: Where the dictionaries leave a passage open, it's translated as the scholars who edited the text read it, and the doubt is given in an endnote, never smoothed over.

[^how-fiction-called-fiction]: Each book's note opens by saying whether it's fiction or fact, and which parts were made up. A book is fact only when none of it was made up, so a history with any legend in it counts as fiction.

[^how-no-borrowed-wording]: Nothing was translated from Malory's English or any modern translation; they were used only to find where a passage sits in the legend.

[^how-source-over-malory]: Where Malory tells a passage differently, the source is the story and his version goes in a note; where sources are joined into one book, the one written first leads.

[^how-story-headings]: Every heading says what happens in its section, in a short plain sentence, so the headings alone tell the story, without giving away how a fight, a trial, a prophecy or a secret turns out.

[^how-laid-out-for-screens]: Laid out as a modern book read on a screen: a new speaker starts a new paragraph, no paragraph runs past 130 words, and the punctuation is a US book's.

[^how-malory-cross-referenced]: Where Malory's *Le Morte d'Arthur* tells the same passage, an endnote names his book and chapters; where it doesn't, nothing is said.

[^how-arthur-story-callouts]: In a history the legend grew from, as Gildas, the *History of the Britons* and the *Welsh Annals*, each person, place or event the Arthur story retells gets a short box in the text, straight after the paragraph that first names it, headed "In the Arthur story" and ending on the asterisk this translation marks its own words with: who or what it becomes in the legend, and in which tellings, so a reader sees how the history feeds the story. The box is this translation's, never the source's.

[^how-no-guessed-identities]: When a figure might be a better-known person from another book, the glossary says so only where the sources do; it never guesses.

[^how-no-common-words-glossed]: No ordinary English word is a glossary entry, since an entry is underlined on every page of every book that shares the glossary.

[^how-free-with-credit]: Anyone may use this book freely, crediting Ryan Allen, under the CC BY 4.0 license this book gives.

## New in this translation

An entry marked with an asterisk was written for this translation, not taken from Giles's index of 1844.
## Achilles

Also: Achillis

The greatest of the Greek heroes at the siege of Troy in Homer's *Iliad*, killed there by the Trojan prince Paris. Geoffrey names him as the father of Pyrrhus, who carried the Trojan captives to Greece.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Achilles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Achilles)

## Áedán mac Gabráin

Also: Ædanum

King of the Irish of Dál Riata, in what's now Argyll in western Scotland, from about 574 CE, the son of Gabrán. Adomnán's *Life of Columba* says Columba ordained him king on Iona, and he led great campaigns until the English of Northumbria beat him at Degsastan in 603 CE. The annals record his death in 607 CE.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Áedán mac Gabráin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C3%81ed%C3%A1n_mac_Gabr%C3%A1in)

## Aeneas

Also: Æneas, Æneæ, Ænea

The Trojan hero who escaped the burning of Troy and, in Roman legend, sailed to Italy and became the ancestor of the Romans. Geoffrey begins the Britons' story with him: he beats Turnus, marries Lavinia and wins the kingdom of Italy, and his great-grandson Brutus is Britain's founder.

Wikipedia: [Aeneas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aeneas)

## Aeneas Silvius

Also: Silvius Æneas

A legendary king of Alba Longa, Aeneas's son, the third king of the Latins. Geoffrey calls him Brutus's uncle and says he reigned in Italy when Brutus founded his city.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Aeneas Silvius](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aeneas_Silvius)

## Aethelberht

Also: Ethelbertus

King of Kent at the end of the sixth century CE, descended from Hengist, and the first English king to become a Christian: he welcomed Augustine's mission from Rome in 597 CE, encouraged by his Christian Frankish wife, Bertha. The history names him in its line of the kings of Kent.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Æthelberht of Kent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C3%86thelberht_of_Kent)

## Aethelfrith

Also: Ethelfridus, Ethelfridum, Ethelfrido

King of the Northumbrians from about 593 to 616 CE, a pagan and the most feared of the English kings of his day. Geoffrey's Ethelfrid falls on the Britons at Chester and kills the monks of Bangor who'd come to pray for them.

Wikipedia: [Æthelfrith](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C3%86thelfrith)

## Africa

Also: Africam, Africana, Africani, Africæ, Africanorum

The continent south of the Mediterranean; to the Romans, chiefly its northern coast. Geoffrey's Trojans reach it after thirty days at sea, still not knowing which way to steer.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Africa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Africa)

## Agag

Also: Agag

The king of the Amalekites in the first book of Samuel. King Saul takes him alive and spares him, against Yahweh's order to destroy the Amalekites and all they own, and the prophet Samuel kills him himself. Bishop Eldad calls Hengist another Agag.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Agag](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agag)

## Aganippus

Also: Aganippus, Aganippo, Aganippum

Cordelia's husband in Geoffrey's story, who marries her with no dowry, wanting only her. He raises an army across Gaul to win Britain back for her father, Leir, and dies soon after.

Wikipedia: [Aganippus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aganippus)

## Agitius

Also: Agitium, Agitio

A Roman commander, three times consul, who gets the Britons' famous letter, "the groans of the Britons," begging for help against their enemies. Geoffrey takes the letter from Gildas; many take Agitius for Aëtius, the Roman general of the 440s CE.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Groans of the Britons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Groans_of_the_Britons)

## Agned

Also: Agned, castellum puellarum

A hill where King Ebraucus builds a town, which Geoffrey says is now called the Girls' Castle, usually taken for Edinburgh. The *History of the Britons* had named Agned as the place of one of Arthur's battles.

Wikipedia: [List of locations associated with Arthurian legend](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_locations_associated_with_Arthurian_legend)

## Akalon

Also: Akalon

A river in Greece near the town of Sparatinum, where the Trojans drive Pandrasus's army into the water. It's known only from Geoffrey's story, and no real river has been securely matched to it.

Wikipedia: [Pandrasus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pandrasus)

## Alan

Also: Alanus, Alano, Alanum

A king of Brittany in Geoffrey's story, Salomon's nephew. He welcomes Cadwaladr when the Britons flee their island, reads the old prophecies with him, and sends Cadwaladr's son and nephew back to rule the Britons who are left.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## Alba Longa

Also: Albam, Albæ

The city in Latium, southeast of Rome, that in Roman legend Aeneas's son Ascanius founded, its kings ruling for centuries before Rome. Geoffrey sets it on the Tiber, though it stood in the Alban Hills, and makes its kings Brutus's relatives.

Wikipedia: [Alba Longa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alba_Longa)

## Alba Silvius

Also: Silvium Albam, Silvii Albæ, patri Albæ

A king of Alba Longa in Roman legend, who follows Latinus Silvius. Geoffrey says Ebraucus's thirty daughters were sent to him to marry Trojans, and that he helped Ebraucus's sons win Germany.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Alba Silvius](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alba_Silvius)

## Alban

Also: Albanus

A Christian of Verulamium, beside today's St Albans, put to death for his faith, Britain's first martyr. Geoffrey tells that he hid his confessor Amphibalus from those hunting Christians, and gave himself up in his place.

Wikipedia: [Saint Alban](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint_Alban)

## Albanactus

Also: Albanactus, Albanacto

Brutus's youngest son in Geoffrey's story. He takes the north of the island and names it Albany after himself. Humber, king of the Huns, lands there, kills him in battle and drives his people south to his brother Locrinus.

Wikipedia: [Albanactus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albanactus)

## Albany

Also: Albaniam, Albaniæ, Albania, Albani, Albanorum

Geoffrey's name for the north of Britain, roughly Scotland, which he says Albanactus named after himself. It comes from *Alba*, the Gaelic name for Scotland.

Wikipedia: [Alba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alba)

## Albion

Also: Albion

The oldest name of Britain, known to the Greeks and Romans, perhaps from the white cliffs of its south coast. Geoffrey says it was the island's name when Brutus came, and that only a few giants lived there.

Wikipedia: [Albion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albion)

## Alclud

Also: Alclud

The rock on the north bank of the Clyde at Dumbarton, the fortress of the Britons of Strathclyde, who called it Alt Clut. Geoffrey says King Ebraucus founded a city there, and Giles's index calls it Dunbritton.

Wikipedia: [Dumbarton Castle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dumbarton_Castle)

## Aldroen

Also: Aldroënus

A king of Brittany in Geoffrey's story, the fourth after Conan Meriadoc. When Archbishop Guithelin begs him to take Britain's crown, he turns it down, calling the island ruined by Rome's yoke, and sends his brother Constantine with two thousand soldiers instead.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Aldroen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aldroen)

## Alexander of Lincoln

Also: Alexander

A bishop of Lincoln from 1123 to his death in 1148 CE, the nephew of Roger of Salisbury, Henry I's chancellor, and schooled at Laon in France. Geoffrey writes Merlin's prophecies to him, saying Alexander pressed him harder than anyone to put them into Latin.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Alexander of Lincoln](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_of_Lincoln)

## Alfred

Also: Aluredus

Alfred the Great, king of the West Saxons from 871 to 899 CE, who had books put into English and gathered older laws into his own law code. Geoffrey says he translated the Molmutine and Marcian laws into English, which no book of his holds.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Alfred the Great](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfred_the_Great)

## Alhfrith

Also: Alfridus

A son of Oswiu, king of the Northumbrians, who ruled Deira under his father and later fell out with him. Geoffrey makes him Oswiu's brother and says he rose against Oswiu with Oethelwald, his nephew.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Alhfrith](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alhfrith)

## Alifantinam

Also: Alifantinam

The king of Spain in Geoffrey's story, one of the rulers of the East who join Lucius Tiberius against Arthur. He leads the first Roman wedge into the great battle with Lucius Catellus, and falls there when Hirelgas rallies the Britons.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## Allectus

Also: Allectum, Allecti

Carausius's treasurer, who murdered him in 293 CE and ruled Britain until Rome won it back in 296. In Geoffrey's story he's an envoy the Roman senate sends with three legions to kill Carausius and take back the kingdom.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Allectus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Allectus)

## Allobroges

Also: Allobrogum, Allobroges

A Gallic people between the Rhône and the Alps, around what's now Geneva and Grenoble, conquered by Rome in 121 BCE. In Geoffrey's story their duke Seginus takes in the exiled Brennius and marries him to his only daughter.

Wikipedia: [Allobroges](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Allobroges)

## Alps

Also: Alpes, Alpium

The great mountain range of Europe, running in an arc from the south of France through Switzerland and northern Italy to Austria and Slovenia. In Merlin's prophecy a cry and the news of a great work carry as far as the Alps.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Alps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alps)

## Altars of the Philaeni

Also: aras Philenorum

A landmark on the coast of Libya, at the bottom of the Gulf of Sidra, that in ancient times marked the border between Carthage's land and Cyrene's, named for two Carthaginian brothers said to have been buried alive there. Geoffrey's Trojans sail past it on their way west.

## Amalek

Also: Amalech

The Amalekites, a desert people of the Hebrew Bible and Israel's old enemy, who attacked the Israelites on their way out of Egypt. Their king, Agag, is the man the prophet Samuel kills after King Saul spares him.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Amalek](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amalek)

## Ambrius

Also: Ambrii

The abbot Geoffrey says founded the monastery near Salisbury, where the British lords murdered at Hengist's peace meeting are buried. Geoffrey seems to read the name of Amesbury, near Stonehenge, as Ambrius's town, and nothing else is known of him.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## Ambrones

Also: redite Ambrones

A Germanic people who fought Rome beside the Cimbri and Teutones in the 100s BCE and were destroyed by Marius in 102 BCE. Cadwaladr names them among the peoples he calls to take the empty island, beside the Saxons.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Ambrones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ambrones)

## Ambrosius Aurelianus

Also: Aurelius Ambrosius, Aurelium Ambrosium, Aurelii Ambrosii, Aurelius, Aurelium, Aurelio, Aurelii

A leader of the Britons against the Saxons, who Geoffrey calls Aurelius Ambrosius and makes a son of King Constantine and the older brother of Uther. Gildas, writing in the 500s CE, names him Ambrosius Aurelianus, the only British leader of his century Gildas names.

Wikipedia: [Ambrosius Aurelianus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ambrosius_Aurelianus)

## Amos

Also: Amos

A herder from Judah sent by Yahweh, in the 700s BCE, to preach against the rich of northern Israel for cheating and crushing the poor. Geoffrey names him with Haggai and Azariah among the prophets of the time of an early British king.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Amos (prophet)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amos_(prophet))

## Amphibalus

Also: Amphibalum, Amphibali

The priest Alban hides from those hunting Christians in Diocletian's day, before Alban gives himself up to die. Gildas tells the story without naming him, and Geoffrey is the first to call him Amphibalus.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Amphibalus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amphibalus)

## Anacletus

Also: Anacletum, Anacletus

Antigonus's companion, a Greek taken prisoner with him by the Trojans at the river Akalon. Pandrasus later calls him his brother, though Geoffrey first named Antigonus so. He's known only from Geoffrey's legend of Brutus.

Wikipedia: [Pandrasus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pandrasus)

## Anaraut

Also: Anaraut

The earl of Salisbury in Geoffrey's story, one of the earls of the great cities who come to Arthur's crown-wearing in the City of the Legions. His name is the Welsh Anarawd, though he isn't the ninth-century king of Gwynedd.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## Anchises

Also: Anchisæ

Aeneas's father in Greek and Roman legend, a prince of the Trojan royal house, who Aeneas carried out of burning Troy on his shoulders. Pandrasus, king of the Greeks, praises Brutus as a young man born of Priam's and Anchises's line.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Anchises](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anchises)

## Andragius

Also: Andragius, Andragii

Cherin's third son in Geoffrey's story, the last of three brothers to reign one after another, and the father of King Urianus. Nothing else is told of him.

Wikipedia: [Andragius](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andragius)

## Androgeus

Also: Androgeus, Androgeo, Androgeum, Androgei

Lud's older son in Geoffrey's story, too young to rule when his father dies, so his uncle Cassivellaunus takes the crown and makes him duke of Kent and gives him Trinovantum. He's drawn from Mandubracius, the British prince who went over to Julius Caesar.

Wikipedia: [Mandubracius](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mandubracius)

## Anjou

Also: Andegavensium, Andegavensis

A region of western France on the lower Loire, around the city of Angers, the old land of the Andecavi. In Geoffrey's story Arthur gives it to his steward Kay once Gaul is won.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [County of Anjou](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/County_of_Anjou)

## Anna daughter of Uther

Also: Annam filiam suam, Anna

The daughter of Uther and Igraine in Geoffrey's story, and Arthur's sister. Her father gives her in marriage to Lot of Lothian, an earl he trusts with his army. Later tellings call her Morgause and make her Igraine's daughter by Gorlois, the mother of Gawain and Mordred.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## Antenor

Also: Antenoris

An old Trojan counselor in Greek and Roman legend who escaped the fall of Troy and, Virgil says, founded Padua in Italy. Geoffrey's Trojans find four families descended from Antenor's companions living on the Tyrrhenian shore, led by Corineus.

Wikipedia: [Antenor (Trojan)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antenor_(Trojan))

## Antigonus

Also: Antigonum, Antigonus, Antigono, Antigoni, Antigonique

Pandrasus's brother, who rallies the fleeing Greeks at the river Akalon and turns on the Trojans rather than drown in flight. He's known only from Geoffrey's legend of Brutus.

Wikipedia: [Pandrasus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pandrasus)

## Antioch

Also: Antiochenam

One of the greatest cities of the Roman east, in Syria, now Antakya in Turkey. Geoffrey says the apostle Peter founded its church before he went on to Rome.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Antioch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antioch)

## Apollo

Also: Apollinis

The Greek and Roman god of light, music, healing and prophecy, a son of Jupiter. Geoffrey puts a temple of his in Trinovantum, and King Bladud dies falling onto it.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Apollo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apollo)

## Apuleius

Also: Apuleius

A Latin writer of the 100s CE from north Africa, best known for his novel the Golden Ass. Maugantius cites his book on the god of Socrates, which says spirits live in the air between the moon and the earth.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Apuleius](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apuleius)

## Aquitaine

Also: Aquitaniam, Aquitania, Aquitaniæ, Aquitanos, Aquitani

The land of southwest France between the Loire, the Pyrenees and the Atlantic. Geoffrey's Trojans land at the mouth of the Loire and lay the country waste, fighting its king Goffarius.

Wikipedia: [Aquitaine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aquitaine)

## Arabia

Also: Arabes

The land of the Arabs, the great peninsula between the Red Sea and the Persian Gulf. In Merlin's prophecy Arabia and Africa fear a warlike boar who carries his charge into the farthest part of Spain.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Arabian Peninsula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arabian_Peninsula)

## Arcadia

Also: Arcadiæ

A mountain region in the middle of the Peloponnese, in southern Greece, held in Greek myth to be the home of Hermes, the god the Romans called Mercury. Merlin's prophecy calls the planet Mercury Stilbon of Arcadia.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Arcadia (region)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arcadia_(region))

## Archbishop Guithelin

Also: Guethelinus, Guethelino

The archbishop of London in Geoffrey's story, who speaks for the Britons when the Romans leave them. He crosses to Brittany to fetch Constantine, brings up his wife and his younger sons, and is dead before Constans is made king. No archbishop of London is known from these years.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Aldroen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aldroen)

## Archgallo

Also: Arthgallo, Arthgalloni, Arthgallonem, Arthgallonis

Gorbonianus's brother in Geoffrey's story, who takes from the rich and raises up ordinary people until the lords throw him off the throne. His brother Elidurus finds him five years later and gives him back the crown, and he then reigns ten years well. Giles prints him *Arthgallo*.

Wikipedia: [Archgallo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archgallo)

## Ariadne

Also: Ariadne

A daughter of King Minos of Crete in Greek myth, who helped Theseus escape the Minotaur's maze and was left by him on the island of Naxos. Merlin's prophecy has her hide among the stars behind a closed door.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Ariadne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ariadne)

## Aries

Also: donec aries

The ram, the first sign of the zodiac, which the sun passes through in spring. In Merlin's prophecy the ram puts its curved horns under the crooked weights of Libra, the scales.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Aries (astrology)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aries_(astrology))

## Ark of the Covenant

Also: arca testamenti

The gold-covered chest that held the tablets of the law given to Moses, kept by the Israelites as the sign of their god's presence. The Bible tells how the Philistines captured it in battle in the days of Eli the priest, and Geoffrey uses that time to date Brutus's founding of New Troy.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Ark of the Covenant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ark_of_the_Covenant)

## Arthgal

Also: Arthgal

The earl of Cargueit, or Warguit, in Geoffrey's story, one of the earls of the great cities at Arthur's crown-wearing in the City of the Legions. Giles's index takes his town for Warwick.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## Arthmail

Also: Arthmail

Blegabred's brother in Geoffrey's story, who reigns after him and is followed by Eldol. Geoffrey tells nothing else of him, and no other source names this king.

## Arthur

Also: Arturo, Arturi, Arturus, Arturum

The king of the Britons whose reign is the heart of this history, the son of Uther Pendragon and Igraine. Geoffrey names him in his first lines as a king whose acts people still tell by heart, though no history had written them down. He's the hero the whole Arthurian legend gathers around, and this book is the first to tell his life.

Wikipedia: [King Arthur](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Arthur)

## Arvirargus

Also: Arviragus, Arviragum, Arvirago, Arviragi

Kymbelinus's younger son in Geoffrey's story, who takes up the fight when his brother Guiderius falls, then makes peace with Claudius and marries his daughter Venissa. Juvenal's satires name an Arviragus, a British king Rome's flatterers hoped to see captured.

Wikipedia: [Arvirargus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arvirargus)

## Asaph

Also: Asaph

The leader of King David's singers in the Bible, whose name heads twelve of the Psalms. Geoffrey names him among the prophets of David's time, with Gad and Nathan.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Asaph (biblical figure)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asaph_(biblical_figure))

## Ascanius

Also: Ascanio, Ascanius, Ascanii

Aeneas's son, who fled Troy with him. In Geoffrey's story he rules after his father, founds Alba on the Tiber and is Brutus's grandfather; it's his soothsayers who predict that the unborn Brutus will kill his father and mother.

Wikipedia: [Ascanius](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ascanius)

## Aschillius

Also: Aschillius, Aschil, Aschillii

The Danes' king in Geoffrey's story, one of the guests at Arthur's crown-wearing in the City of the Legions. He comes with the kings of the other islands, and Geoffrey tells nothing more of him here.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## Asclepiodotus

Also: Asclepiodotus, Asclepiodotum, Asclepiodoti, Asclepiodoto

Julius Asclepiodotus, the Roman prefect who beat Allectus and won Britain back for Rome in 296 CE. Geoffrey makes him a Briton, duke of Cornwall, crowned king by the Britons to fight Allectus.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Julius Asclepiodotus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julius_Asclepiodotus)

## Assarach

Also: Assarach, Assaraco

One of King Ebraucus's twenty sons in Geoffrey's story, who leads his brothers by sea to Germany. With the help of Alba Silvius, king of the Latins, they conquer its people and take the kingdom.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Ebraucus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ebraucus)

## Assaracus

Also: Assaracus, Assaraci

A young Greek noble, born of a Trojan mother, who sides with the enslaved Trojans because his brother is trying to take the three castles their father left him. Geoffrey's Assaracus isn't the Trojan king of that name in Greek myth.

Wikipedia: [Pandrasus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pandrasus)

## Aube

Also: Albam fluvium

A river of northeastern France that flows into the Seine. In Geoffrey's story Arthur camps on its bank and sends his envoys from there to order Lucius Tiberius out of Gaul.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Aube](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aube)

## Auguselus

Also: Auguselus, Auguselo

A king of the Scots in Geoffrey's story, brother of Lot and Urien, whose family ruled the north before the Saxons came. Arthur gives him back the kingship of the Scots, and he's king of Albany at Arthur's court.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Ywain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ywain)

## Augustine of Canterbury

Also: Augustinus, Augustino

The monk Pope Gregory sent in 597 CE to turn the English to Christ, who became the first archbishop of Canterbury. Geoffrey tells that he asked the British bishops to submit to him and join his mission to the English.

Wikipedia: [Augustine of Canterbury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Augustine_of_Canterbury)

## Augustus

Also: Augustus Cæsar

In Geoffrey's story, the emperor who brings up Kymbelinus at his court, so that the young king pays Rome's tribute of his own free will. Christ is born in his reign.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Augustus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Augustus)

## Aurelius Caninus

Also: Aurelius Conanus, est a Conano

A king of Britain in Geoffrey's story, Constantine's nephew, who kills Constantine and takes the crown after him. He throws his uncle into prison, kills that uncle's two sons, and dies in the second year of his reign. Geoffrey takes him from Gildas's Aurelius Caninus, whose love of civil war he keeps.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Aurelius Conanus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aurelius_Conanus)

## Autun

Also: Augustodunum

A town of Burgundy in eastern France, founded by the Romans as Augustodunum. In Geoffrey's story Arthur marches toward it, thinking Lucius Tiberius is there, and Lucius thinks of falling back into it to wait for help.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Autun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Autun)

## Avalon

Also: Avallonis

The island where, Geoffrey says, Arthur's sword was forged. Geoffrey gives no more of it here, and doesn't say where it lies. It's the island of the later legend that Glastonbury's monks claimed for their own.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Avalon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Avalon)

## Azara

Also: montes Azaræ

Mountains on the North African coast where pirates attack the Trojans and are beaten. Giles's index places them only in Africa; no real range has been securely matched to them.

## Azariah

Also: Azarias

A prophet of the Bible, the son of Oded, who told King Asa of Judah that Yahweh would stay with him only as long as he stayed with Yahweh. Geoffrey names him with Haggai and Amos among the prophets of the time of an early British king.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Azariah (prophet)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Azariah_(prophet))

## Babylon

Also: Babyloniæ, Babyloniensis

The great ancient city on the Euphrates, in what's now Iraq, south of Baghdad. In Geoffrey's story its king, Micipsa, marches with Lucius Tiberius against Arthur and falls in the great battle.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Babylon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Babylon)

## Baldulf

Also: Baldulphus

Colgrin's brother, a Saxon leader in Geoffrey's story. While Arthur besieges Colgrin in York, Baldulf shaves his hair and beard and passes through the British camp as a harper, so the men on the walls can pull him up to his brother.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## Bangor-on-Dee

Also: Bangor, Bangornensium

A village on the river Dee in northeast Wales, near Wrexham, where a great monastery stood in the 600s CE. Bede tells of its many monks, and Geoffrey of its abbot Dinoot, who refuses Augustine, and of the monks Aethelfrith kills. It's another place than Deiniol's Bangor.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Bangor-on-Dee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bangor-on-Dee)

## Barclenses

Also: Barclenses

The name Geoffrey gives Partholón's people, exiles from Spain who sail the seas for a year and a half before Gurguit Barbtruc settles them in Ireland. No people of that name is known outside Geoffrey's story.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## Bassianus

Also: Bassianus, Bassianum, Bassiano

The emperor known as Caracalla, born Lucius Septimius Bassianus, Severus's son, who ruled from 198 to 217 CE. In Geoffrey's story his mother is a Briton, so the Britons choose him as king over his brother Geta.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Caracalla](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caracalla)

## Bath, Somerset

Also: Kaerbadum, Badus, now called Bath, at Bath, builds Bath, Badonis balnea, Bath's baths, pagum Badonis, Badone, district of Bath, Urgennius of Bath, sets it at Bath

The spa city in Somerset, Aquae Sulis to the Romans, built around hot springs and a temple to the goddess Sulis Minerva. Geoffrey says King Bladud founded it as Kaerbadum and made its baths.

Wikipedia: [Bath, Somerset](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bath,_Somerset)

## Bayeux

Also: Bajocas

A town of Normandy in northern France, famous for its tapestry of the Norman Conquest. In Geoffrey's story it's Bedivere's city, built by his great-grandfather, and he's buried there beside its wall.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Bayeux](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bayeux)

## Bede

Also: Beda

The Northumbrian monk of Jarrow, the most learned man of his age in western Europe, whose *Ecclesiastical History of the English People*, finished in 731 CE, is the main history of England's early centuries. Geoffrey names him with Gildas as the historians who said nothing of Britain's kings before Christ, nor of Arthur.

Wikipedia: [Bede](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bede)

## Bedivere

Also: Beduero, Beduerum, Beduerus, Bedueri, Beduerumque

Arthur's butler in Geoffrey's story, the officer who served the king's wine, a great office at a royal court. When Gaul is won, Arthur gives him Neustria, now Normandy. He's the Bedwyr of the Welsh tales, one of Arthur's first companions.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Bedivere](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bedivere)

## Belinus

Also: Belinus, Belino, Belinum, Belini

Dunvallo Molmutius's older son in Geoffrey's story, who takes the crown and the south of Britain while his brother Brennius holds the north. After their mother makes peace between them, the two lead their armies across Gaul and take Rome, and Belinus comes home to build roads and cities.

Wikipedia: [Belinus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Belinus)

## Belinus the general

Also: Belinus princeps militiæ

The commander of Cassivellaunus's army in Geoffrey's story, whose advice the king follows in everything when Julius Caesar lands. He shares his name with the earlier King Belinus, and Geoffrey tells nothing more of him.

## Billingsgate

Also: Belinesgata

A water gate and wharf on the Thames below London Bridge, later famous for its fish market. Geoffrey says Belinus built it with a tower over it and named it after himself, but its name probably comes from an Englishman called Billing.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Billingsgate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billingsgate)

## Bithynia

Also: Bithyniæ, Bithyniæque

An ancient region of northwest Asia Minor, now in Turkey, along the Sea of Marmara and the Black Sea. In Geoffrey's story its duke, Polytetes, marches with Lucius Tiberius and dies by Arthur's hand.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Bithynia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bithynia)

## Bladud

Also: Bladud

Hudibras's son in Geoffrey's story, a clever king who builds Bath with its hot baths and teaches magic across Britain. He makes himself wings and tries to fly, and is killed falling onto the temple of Apollo in Trinovantum.

Wikipedia: [Bladud](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bladud)

## Bledericus

Also: Bledericus

The duke of Cornwall in Geoffrey's story, one of the British leaders who drive Aethelfrith back from Bangor. He leads the Britons in those battles and falls in the last of them.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## Bledudo

Also: Bleduno

The king after Merianus in Geoffrey's list of the kings of Britain. Geoffrey tells nothing of him but his name and his place in the line, and Giles prints it *Bleduno*.

Wikipedia: [Bledudo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bledudo)

## Blegabred

Also: Blegabred

A king in Geoffrey's list who outdoes every singer before him at melody and on every instrument, so people call him the god of entertainers. His brother Arthmail reigns after him, and Blegabred is known from Geoffrey alone.

## Boccus

Also: Boccus, Bocco, Boccum

The king of the Medes in Geoffrey's story, an ally of Lucius Tiberius. In the great battle his lance kills Bedivere, and Bedivere's nephew Hirelgas cuts his way to him, kills him and tears his body apart.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## Boeotia

Also: Bœotiæ

A region of central Greece, north of Athens, with Thebes as its old chief city. In Geoffrey's story its ruler, Aethion, is one of the lords of the East who march with Lucius Tiberius.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Boeotia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boeotia)

## Borellus

Also: Borellus, Borellum

The lord of Le Mans in Geoffrey's story, one of the lords from overseas at Arthur's crown-wearing in the City of the Legions. Geoffrey tells nothing more of him here.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## Boso

Also: Boso, Bosonem, Bosoni

The earl of Ridoc, which Geoffrey says is Oxford, one of the earls of the great cities who come to Arthur's crown-wearing in the City of the Legions. Geoffrey tells nothing more of him here.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## Boulogne

Also: Boloniæ, Boloniensis

Boulogne-sur-Mer, a port of northern France on the Channel, the Romans' Gesoriacum, from which their fleets sailed for Britain. In Geoffrey's story its earl, Leodegarius, comes to Arthur's court.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Boulogne-sur-Mer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boulogne-sur-Mer)

## Brennius

Also: Brennius, Brennium, Brennii, Brennio, Brenni

Dunvallo Molmutius's younger son in Geoffrey's story, who holds Britain north of the Humber under his brother Belinus. Beaten and driven out, he marries the heir of the Allobroges, makes peace with Belinus through their mother and takes Rome with him. Geoffrey makes him the Gaulish chief Brennus, who sacked Rome.

Wikipedia: [Brennius](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brennius)

## Brian

Also: Brianum, Brianus, Briano, Brianumque

Cadwallon's nephew in Geoffrey's story. His tears turn Cadwallon against Edwin, he feeds the starving king a piece of his own thigh on Guernsey, and he kills Edwin's seer Pellitus at York in a beggar's clothes.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## Bricel

Also: Bricelem

A companion of Gorlois, duke of Cornwall, in Geoffrey's story. Merlin takes Bricel's shape himself on the night he brings Uther into Tintagel looking like Gorlois, so the guards will know the duke's men. Geoffrey names him only here.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## Britael

Also: Britael

One of the three kings under Cassivellaunus in Geoffrey's story who urge him to attack Julius Caesar's camp at once. Geoffrey makes him king of Dyfed. He's known only from Geoffrey.

Wikipedia: [List of kings in Wales from the Matter of Britain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_kings_in_Wales_from_the_Matter_of_Britain)

## Britain

Also: Britannia, Britanniæ, Britanniam

The island of Great Britain, holding today's England, Wales and Scotland. Geoffrey opens by praising it as the best of islands, eight hundred miles long and two hundred wide, rich in metals, fields, woods and rivers. He says it was called Albion until Brutus named it after himself.

Wikipedia: [Great Britain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Britain)

## Britons

Also: Britones, Britonum, Britannis, Britonibus, Britannorum, Britonumque, Britonesque

The Celtic people of Britain, the ancestors of the Welsh, the Cornish and the Bretons, whose kings this history follows. Geoffrey says they once held the whole island from sea to sea, until for their pride they gave way to the Picts and the Saxons. In his story they take their name from Brutus, their first king.

Wikipedia: [Celtic Britons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celtic_Britons)

## Brittany

Also: Armorica, Armoricam, Armoricum, Letavia, Armorici, Armoricosque, Armoricanos, minorem Britanniam, Armorico, Armoricanum, Armoricana Britannia, Armoricanis, Armoricanorum, Armoricæ, Armoricanam

The peninsula of northwest France, the Roman Armorica, where Britons crossing from Britain settled in the 400s and 500s CE, giving it its name and its Celtic language. Geoffrey says Maximianus gave it to Conan Meriadoc and his British soldiers, and called it a second Britain.

Wikipedia: [Brittany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brittany)

## Brocmail

Also: Brocmail

The earl of Chester in Geoffrey's story, who holds out against Aethelfrith's army with fewer men, then flees. Bede tells the same battle at Chester, and the man is taken for Brochwel Ysgythrog, a king of Powys.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## Brutus

Also: Brutus, Bruti, Bruto, Brutum

In Geoffrey's story, the great-grandson of Aeneas who shoots his father by accident and frees the Trojans enslaved in Greece. He sails west on the goddess Diana's word, settles the island he names Britain after himself, and founds New Troy on the Thames and is the first of the kings Geoffrey counts down to Arthur. The Brutus Greenshield of Part 2 is another man.

Wikipedia: [Brutus of Troy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brutus_of_Troy)

## Brutus Greenshield

Also: Viride-scutum, Viridescutum

One of Ebraucus's sons in Geoffrey's story, who stays in Britain when his brothers sail for Germany and reigns twelve years after his father. His name is the Latin *Viride-scutum*, "green shield."

Wikipedia: [Brutus Greenshield](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brutus_Greenshield)

## Budic II

Also: Budecius

The king of Brittany in Geoffrey's story who takes in the boys Aurelius Ambrosius and Uther when their guardians flee Vortigern, and raises them with honor. Budic II was a real king of Cornouaille, in the west of Brittany, in the late 400s and early 500s CE.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Budic II of Brittany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Budic_II_of_Brittany)

## Burne

Also: Burne

The place where Penda kills Oswald in Geoffrey's story. Bede calls the battle Maserfield and sets it in 642 CE, and where Geoffrey's name for it comes from isn't known.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## Cadfan

Also: Caduanus, Caduanum, Caduano, Caduani

A king of Gwynedd in northwest Wales in the early 600s CE, and Cadwallon's father. In Geoffrey's story the Britons crown him at Leicester, and he shares Britain with Aethelfrith at the Humber. His memorial stone still stands in a church on Anglesey.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Cadfan ap Iago](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cadfan_ap_Iago)

## Cador

Also: Cadorem, Cador, Cadoris

The duke of Cornwall in Geoffrey's story, Arthur's ally in his first wars against the Saxons, who raised Guinevere in his household. He's a figure of Welsh tradition, called Cado in the Welsh genealogies, though he may be Geoffrey's own invention.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Cador](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cador)

## Cadwaladr

Also: Cadwaladrum, Cadwalladrus, Cadwalladrum, Cadwalladri, Cadwalladro

A king of the Britons of the 600s CE, Cadwallon's son, the last king Geoffrey's history reaches. Geoffrey says the old British book he translated ran from Brutus to him. Welsh tradition remembered him as the last Briton to claim the crown of the whole island.

Wikipedia: [Cadwaladr ap Cadwallon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cadwaladr_ap_Cadwallon)

## Cadwallon ap Cadfan

Also: Cadwalonis, Cadwallo, Cadwallonem, Cadwalloni, Cadwallonis, Cadwallone, Caduallo

A king of Gwynedd, in north Wales, in the 600s CE, named in Geoffrey's first lines as the father of the last king his book reaches. He's the one British king of his age who fought his way deep into the English kingdoms, and Geoffrey makes him king of all Britain.

Wikipedia: [Cadwallon ap Cadfan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cadwallon_ap_Cadfan)

## Cadwallon Lawhir

Also: Caduallo Leuirh

A king of Gwynedd, in north Wales, around 500 CE, the grandson of Cunedda, remembered for driving the last Irish settlers off Anglesey. Geoffrey makes him one of the kings at Arthur's crown-wearing in the City of the Legions.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Cadwallon Lawhir](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cadwallon_Lawhir)

## Caen

Also: Camum

A city of Normandy in northern France, a few miles inland from the coast. In Geoffrey's story it's the town Kay founded, where he's carried after the great battle and dies of his wound.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Caen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caen)

## Caerleon

Also: Kaerosc, urbs Legionum, urbe Legionum, City of the Legions, urbis Legionum, urbem Legionum

The town on the Usk in south Wales whose Welsh name means the fortress of the legion. Rome's Second Legion was based there from about 75 CE. Geoffrey says Belinus founded it as Kaerosc and the Romans renamed it the City of the Legions, though Giles's index takes Kaerosc for Newport.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Caerleon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caerleon)

## Caithness

Also: Cathenesiam, Cathenesium, Cathenesia, Catanesium

The far northeastern tip of mainland Scotland, facing Orkney across the Pentland Firth. Geoffrey says Marganus's share of Britain ran from the Humber toward it.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Caithness](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caithness)

## Calaterium

Also: Calaterium, Calatherio, Calaterio

A forest in the north of Britain in Geoffrey's story, where Belinus beats Brennius's Norwegians and where Elidurus later meets his brother Archgallo. Giles's index takes it for Galtres, the old royal forest north of York, but Brennius has landed in Albany, so Geoffrey may have meant a wood further north.

Wikipedia: [Belinus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Belinus)

## Camber

Also: Kamber, Kambrum

Brutus's third son in Geoffrey's story. He takes the land beyond the Severn. Geoffrey says it was called Cambria after him and is now Wales. He helps his brother Locrinus drive Humber the Hun out of the north.

Wikipedia: [King Camber](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Camber)

## Camlann

Also: Cambula

The river in Cornwall where Mordred waits for Arthur, which Giles's index takes for the Camel, near Camelford. The Welsh annals call the battle there Camlann.

Wikipedia: [Battle of Camlann](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Camlann)

## Canterbury

Also: Kaerlem, Kantuariam, Doroberniam, Doroberniæ, Cantuaria, Dorobernia

The cathedral city in Kent, the seat of England's chief archbishop since Augustine came there in 597 CE. Geoffrey says King Hudibras founded it and called it Kaerlem.

Wikipedia: [Canterbury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canterbury)

## Capoir

Also: cui Capoir, Capoiri

The king after Pir in Geoffrey's list of the kings of Britain, and the father of Digueillus, who succeeds him. Geoffrey tells nothing else of him but his name.

Wikipedia: [Capoir](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capoir)

## Capys

Also: Capys filius

A king of Alba Longa in Roman legend, the son of the king Geoffrey calls Silvius Epitus. Geoffrey dates the eagle's speech at Shaftesbury by his reign.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Capys](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capys)

## Caradoc of Llancarfan

Also: Karadoco Lancarbanensi

A Welsh churchman of the 1100s CE, the author of Lives of Gildas and other saints, who lived in Geoffrey's own day. Geoffrey leaves the later kings of the Welsh to him to write about.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Caradoc of Llancarfan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caradoc_of_Llancarfan)

## Caradocus

Also: Caradocus, Caradoco

Duke of Cornwall in Geoffrey's story under King Octavius, who advises the king to marry his daughter to the senator Maximianus and sends his own son Mauricius to Rome to fetch him. He's known only from Geoffrey.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Caradocus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caradocus)

## Carausius

Also: Carausius, Carausii, Carausio

A Roman naval commander of low birth who in 286 CE took power in Britain and northern Gaul and ruled them as emperor. In Geoffrey's story he's a young Briton who wins a fleet from the Roman senate to guard the coast, then turns it to his own ends.

Wikipedia: [Carausius](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carausius)

## Careticus

Also: Careticus, Careticum, Caretico

A king of the Britons in Geoffrey's story, Maelgwn's successor, who loves civil war. The Saxons bring Gormund and his Africans against him, and he's besieged in Cirencester and driven beyond the Severn into Wales.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Keredic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keredic)

## Cargueit

Also: Cargueitensis, Warguit

The town of Earl Arthgal in Geoffrey's story, which he says is also called Warguit. Giles's index takes it for Warwick, in the English Midlands, "probably", and nothing in the story settles it.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## Carlisle

Also: vocatam Kaerleir, Kaerleil

The city in Cumbria near the Scottish border, Luguvalium to the Romans. Geoffrey says King Leil built it and named it Kaerleil after himself, though Giles prints the name *Kaerleir* in the text.

Wikipedia: [Carlisle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carlisle)

## Carmarthen

Also: Kaermodin

A town on the river Towy in the southwest of Wales, Caerfyrddin in Welsh, the Romans' Moridunum. Geoffrey calls it Kaermodin, and there Vortigern's messengers find the fatherless boy Merlin, the name read as Merlin's fort.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Carmarthen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carmarthen)

## Cassivellaunus

Also: Cassibellauni, Cassibellaunum, Cassibellaunus, Cassibellauno

A king of the Britons, Lud's brother, who fought Julius Caesar when the Romans invaded. He's the real British war leader Caesar names in his own account of his invasions of 55 and 54 BCE.

Wikipedia: [Cassivellaunus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cassivellaunus)

## Catellus

Also: Catellus filius, Post Catellum

Gerennus's son in Geoffrey's story, who succeeds his father as king of Britain. Geoffrey tells nothing of him but his name and his place in the line of kings.

Wikipedia: [Catellus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catellus)

## Catigern

Also: Katigernus, Catigernus

One of Vortigern's three sons, named with his brothers Vortimer and Pascentius. Geoffrey says he and Horsa killed each other at the ford of Episford, in Vortimer's second battle against the Saxons.

Wikipedia: [Catigern](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catigern)

## Celidon Wood

Also: Caledonis

A forest of northern Britain, the Coed Celyddon of Welsh tradition, usually taken for the Caledonian Forest of southern Scotland. Merlin's prophecy names it, and the *History of the Britons* sets one of Arthur's battles there.

## Chartres

Also: Carnotensis, Carnotensi

A city of north central France, southwest of Paris, famous for its cathedral. In Geoffrey's story its earl, Guerinus, leads the twelve peers of Gaul to Arthur's court.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Chartres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chartres)

## Cheldric

Also: Cheldrici, Cheldrico, Cheldericus, Cheldricum, Cheldricus

A Saxon duke in Geoffrey's story who sails from Germany with six hundred ships to help Colgrin and Baldulf against Arthur. Wikipedia's Battle of Badon notes that some scholars took him for Cerdic, the first king of Wessex.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Battle of Badon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Badon)

## Chelianus

Also: Chelianus

A famous priest of Llandaff in Geoffrey's story, who Arthur appoints archbishop of Dol with King Hoel's agreement. San-Marte notes the Welsh Brut Tysilio calls him Teilo, bishop of Llandaff.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## Cherdic

Also: Cerdich

A Saxon leader who comes over with Octa and Ebissa and three hundred ships, at Hengist's invitation. Geoffrey tells nothing more of him here, and some take him for Cerdic, the first king of the West Saxons.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Ambrosius Aurelianus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ambrosius_Aurelianus)

## Cherin

Also: Cherin

Porrex II's successor in Geoffrey's story, and the father of three sons, Fulgenius, Edadus and Andragius, who all reign one after another. Nothing else is told of him.

Wikipedia: [Cherin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cherin)

## Chester

Also: venerunt Legecestriam

A Roman fortress town on the River Dee, in northwest England, which the Britons called Cair Legion, the City of the Legions. The annals record the battle there in 613 CE, when Aethelfrith of Northumbria beat the Britons and, Bede says, killed hundreds of monks from Bangor who'd come to pray for them.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Chester](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chester)

## Cheulfus

Also: Cheulfo

A duke of the Morini in Geoffrey's story who lands in Britain again and again, until Brennius drives him out each time. The men who turn Brennius against his brother remind him of it, and Cheulfus is known only from this line of Geoffrey's.

## Cicero

Also: Tulliano

Marcus Tullius Cicero, the Roman speaker, lawyer and statesman of the first century BCE, the model of Latin style for every medieval schoolboy. Hoel praises Arthur's speech as sweetened with Cicero's honey.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Cicero](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cicero)

## Cirencester

Also: Cirecestriam

A market town in Gloucestershire, in western England, that was one of the largest towns of Roman Britain. In Geoffrey's story Gormund besieges King Careticus there, then takes the town and burns it.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Cirencester](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cirencester)

## Claudius

Also: Claudius, Claudii, Claudium, Claudio, Claudii Cæsaris

In Geoffrey's story, the emperor who invades Britain when Guiderius refuses the tribute. He makes peace with Arvirargus by giving him his daughter, takes Orkney and founds Gloucester.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Claudius](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Claudius)

## Cledaucus

Also: Cledancus

The king after Eliud in Geoffrey's list of the kings of Britain. Geoffrey tells nothing of him but his name and his place in the line, and Giles prints it *Cledancus*.

Wikipedia: [Cledaucus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cledaucus)

## Cloarius

Also: Cloarius

The hill above the river Wye where Vortigern's last fort, Genoreu, stands in Geoffrey's story. Giles's index calls it a hill on the Wye, and Wikipedia's Ambrosius Aurelianus places the fort at the hill fort of Little Doward, in Herefordshire, England.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## Cloten

Also: Clotenis

A king of Cornwall in Geoffrey's story, in the years of civil war after Ferrex and Porrex, and the father of Dunvallo Molmutius. Nothing more is told of him.

Wikipedia: [Dyfnwal Moelmud](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dyfnwal_Moelmud)

## Clotenus

Also: Cletonus

The king after Cledaucus in Geoffrey's list of the kings of Britain. Geoffrey tells nothing of him but his name and his place in the line, and Giles prints it *Cletonus*.

Wikipedia: [Clotenus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clotenus)

## Cnut

Also: urbe Canuti nemoris

Cnut the Great, a Danish king who took England in 1016 CE and ruled it until his death in 1035 CE, as well as Denmark and Norway. San-Marte reads the city of Cnut's forest in Merlin's prophecy as named for him, so the line is later than his reign.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Cnut](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cnut)

## Coel

Also: Coel

The duke of Colchester in Geoffrey's story who rises against King Asclepiodotus and takes the crown, then makes peace with Rome and gives his daughter Helena to Constantius. Welsh tradition knows him as Coel Hen, and the nursery rhyme as Old King Cole.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Coel Hen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coel_Hen)

## Coillus

Also: Post Coillum

The king after Catellus in Geoffrey's list of the kings of Britain, followed by Porrex II. Geoffrey tells nothing of him but his name, and Wikipedia's article calls him Millus.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Millus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Millus)

## Coillus son of Marius

Also: nomine Coillus, Coillo filius, ipse Coillus

Marius's son in Geoffrey's story, brought up in Rome, who pays its tribute and keeps the peace, and fathers Lucius, the first Christian king. Welsh tradition knows Lucius's father as Coel.

## Colchester

Also: Kaercolvin, Colecestriæ

The town in Essex, in eastern England, Camulodunum to the Romans and the first capital of Roman Britain. Geoffrey gives it the British name Kaercolvin and makes it the seat of Duke Coel.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Colchester](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colchester)

## Colgrin

Also: Colgrino, Colgrinum, Colgrinus

A Saxon leader in Geoffrey's story who, after Uther's death, brings his countrymen from Germany to wipe out the Britons. The young Arthur beats him on the river Douglas and besieges him in York, where his brother Baldulf slips in to him dressed as a harper.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## Conan Meriadoc

Also: Conanum, Conanus, Conano, Conani, Meriadocum, Meriadocus, Meriadoci, Meriadoco

King Octavius's nephew in Geoffrey's story, who hopes to inherit the throne of Britain and is furious when it goes to Maximianus instead. Breton legend holds him to be the founder of Brittany's line of kings.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Conan Meriadoc](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conan_Meriadoc)

## Concord

Also: Concordiæ

The Roman goddess of agreement and harmony, Concordia, who had a famous temple in the Forum at Rome. Geoffrey says Dunvallo built a temple of Concord in Trinovantum to confirm his laws and was buried beside it.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Concordia (mythology)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Concordia_(mythology))

## Conisbrough

Also: Kaerconan, urbem Conani, Cunungeburg

A town in South Yorkshire, England, between Doncaster and Rotherham, known for its Norman castle. Geoffrey calls it Kaerconan, "Conan's town," and says it's now called Cunungeburg. Hengist, fleeing Aurelius, turns to fight him outside it.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Conisbrough](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conisbrough)

## Constans II

Also: Constans, Constantem, proveniret Constanti

Constantine's oldest son in Geoffrey's story, given as a boy to the church of Amphibalus at Winchester to be a monk. After his father's death Vortigern takes him out of the monastery, makes him king, rules through him and plots his murder by the Picts of his court. Historians take him from the son of the usurper Constantine III, a monk his father made co-emperor.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## Constantine III

Also: Constantinum fratrem meum, vocatoque Constantino, erexerunt Constantinum, Defuncto igitur Constantino

Aldroen's brother in Geoffrey's story, a prince of Brittany sent with two thousand soldiers to save Britain. The Britons crown him at Silchester, and he fathers Constans, Aurelius Ambrosius and Uther Pendragon before a Pict stabs him. Historians take him from the soldier Rome's army in Britain made emperor in 407 CE.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Constantine III (Western Roman emperor)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constantine_III_(Western_Roman_emperor))

## Constantine the Great

Also: Constantinus, Constantinum, Constantini, Constantino, Constantine

The Roman emperor from 306 to 337 CE, who made Christianity legal. In Geoffrey's story he's the son of Constantius and the British Helena, king of Britain after his father, who goes to Rome to overthrow Maxentius.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Constantine the Great](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constantine_the_Great)

## Constantius

Also: Constantius, Constantium

Constantius Chlorus, a Roman senator and general who became emperor of the western provinces and died at York in 306 CE. In Geoffrey's story Rome sends him to win Britain back from King Coel, after he's already won Spain for Rome.

Wikipedia: [Constantius Chlorus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constantius_Chlorus)

## Conwenna

Also: Conwenna

The mother of Belinus and Brennius in Geoffrey's story, Dunvallo Molmutius's widow. As her sons' armies are about to fight, she walks out between the lines, bares her breasts to Brennius and talks him into making peace with his brother.

Wikipedia: [Belinus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Belinus)

## Cordelia

Also: Cordeillam, Cordeilla, Cordeillæ

Leir's youngest daughter in Geoffrey's story, who won't flatter him. He marries her off with no land or money to Aganippus, king of the Franks. She takes her father in when her sisters drive him out, rules Britain after him for five years, and kills herself in her nephews' prison.

Wikipedia: [Cordelia of Britain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cordelia_of_Britain)

## Corineus

Also: Corineo, Corineus, Corineum, Corinei

The leader of four families of Trojan exiles living by the Tyrrhenian Sea, a modest man, wise in advice, bold and strong enough to beat any giant as if fighting a boy. He joins Brutus with his people and fights beside him in every battle.

Wikipedia: [Corineus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corineus)

## Cornish

Also: Cornubiensis, Corineeinsem, Corineensium, Cornubiensium

The people of Cornwall, at the southwest tip of Britain, who spoke a Celtic language close to Welsh and Breton. Geoffrey says Corineus's followers were later called Cornish after him, and fought beside Brutus in every battle.

Wikipedia: [Cornish people](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cornish_people)

## Cornwall

Also: Cornubia, Cornubiam, Cornubiæ, Corineam, Corinea, Cornubico

The peninsula at the southwest tip of Britain. Geoffrey says Corineus chose it for his share of the island because it held the most giants to fight, and called it Corinea after himself; its name now comes either from the island's horn, *cornu*, or from that name worn down.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Cornwall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cornwall)

## Crete

Also: Cretæ

The largest island of Greece, in the eastern Mediterranean south of the Aegean Sea. In Geoffrey's story its ruler, Hippolytus, is one of the lords of the East who march with Lucius Tiberius.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Crete](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crete)

## Cridious

Also: Cridious

One of the three kings under Cassivellaunus in Geoffrey's story who urge him to attack Julius Caesar's camp at once. Geoffrey makes him king of Albany. He's known only from Geoffrey.

## Crocea Mors

Also: Crocea mors

Julius Caesar's sword in Geoffrey's story, which sticks in Nennius's shield when the two fight and is buried with him. Its name means yellow death, because nobody it wounded lived.

Wikipedia: [Nennius of Britain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nennius_of_Britain)

## Cuelinus

Also: Evelinus, Evelinum, Evelino

Androgeus's nephew in Geoffrey's story, who kills the king's nephew Hirelglas after they quarrel over a wrestling match. Androgeus refuses to hand him over, and calls Julius Caesar back to Britain. Giles prints his name Evelinus.

Wikipedia: [Mandubracius](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mandubracius)

## Cunedagius

Also: Cunedagius, Cunedagium, Cunedagio, Cunedagii

Regan and Henwinus's son in Geoffrey's story, who with his cousin Marganus overthrows his aunt Cordelia. He beats Marganus when Marganus attacks him, rules all of Britain for thirty-three years, and is the father of Rivallo.

Wikipedia: [Cunedagius](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cunedagius)

## Cursalem

Also: Cursalem

The earl of Kaicester in Geoffrey's story, one of the earls of the great cities who come to Arthur's crown-wearing in the City of the Legions. Giles's index takes his town for Chichester.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## Dabutius

Also: Dabutius

The boy who quarrels with Merlin at Carmarthen and taunts him for having no father, boasting of his own royal blood on both sides. His taunt shows Vortigern's messengers the boy they've been sent to find. He's known only from Geoffrey.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## Danaans

Also: Danaos

One of Homer's names for the Greeks who fought at Troy, after Danaus, a legendary king of Argos. Mempricius the Trojan uses it for the Greeks the Trojans would have to live among if they stayed.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Names of the Greeks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Names_of_the_Greeks)

## Danes

Also: Dacorum, Dacos, Dacis

The people of Denmark. Geoffrey calls them *Daci*, the Latin name of the Dacians of the lower Danube, which writers of his day used for the Danes, and in his story their king Guichtlac fights Brennius at sea and then pays Belinus tribute.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Danes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Danes)

## Danius

Also: Danius

Kinarius's brother in Geoffrey's story, who succeeds him as king of Britain. His son Morvidus, by his mistress Tangustela, takes the throne after him and becomes famous for his cruelty.

Wikipedia: [Danius](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Danius)

## Dardanus

Also: Dardani

In Greek myth, a son of Zeus who founded the royal line of Troy, so that the Trojans were sometimes called Dardanians after him. Brutus's letter to the king of the Greeks calls his people a nation sprung from Dardanus's famous line.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Dardanus (son of Zeus)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dardanus_(son_of_Zeus))

## David

Also: David regis avunculus, Saint David, archiepiscopus David

Saint David, the patron saint of Wales. In Geoffrey's story he's Arthur's uncle, whose life is an example of goodness to everyone he teaches, and he's made archbishop of the City of the Legions when Dubricius retires.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Saint David](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint_David)

## Deiniol

Also: sanctus Daniel Bangornensis

The first bishop of Bangor, in north Wales, in the sixth century CE, who founded the monastery there that grew into Bangor Cathedral. The annals record his burial in 584 CE, and he's still remembered as a saint in Wales.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Deiniol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deiniol)

## Deira

Also: Deira, Deiram, Deiri

An English kingdom around York, between the Humber and the Tees, in the 500s and 600s CE. Geoffrey uses its name for that northern country even in the reigns of the old British kings.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Deira](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deira)

## Denmark

Also: Daciæ, Daciam

The kingdom between the North Sea and the Baltic, south of Norway. Geoffrey calls it Dacia, and in his story Belinus lets its king go home in return for tribute, and Belinus's son Gurguit Barbtruc conquers it again when its king stops paying.

Wikipedia: [Denmark](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denmark)

## Deruvian

Also: Duvianum

Fagan's companion in Geoffrey's story, sent by Pope Eleutherius to baptize Lucius and turn the Britons' temples into churches. Giles prints his name Duvianus, and Welsh churches honor him as a saint.

Wikipedia: [Deruvian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deruvian)

## Diana

Also: Dianæ

The Roman goddess of hunting, the woods and the moon, Artemis to the Greeks. In Geoffrey's story her image in a ruined temple on Leogecia answers Brutus's prayer and tells him of an island beyond Gaul where his people will live.

Wikipedia: [Diana (mythology)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diana_(mythology))

## Digueillus

Also: Gligueillus

Capoir's son in Geoffrey's story, a modest, sensible king who does fairer justice than anyone, and the father of Heli, who reigns after him. Giles prints him *Gligueillus*.

Wikipedia: [Digueillus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Digueillus)

## Dimilioc

Also: Dimilioc

The castle in Cornwall where Gorlois, duke of Cornwall, holds out against King Uther in Geoffrey's story, keeping his wife Igraine apart at Tintagel. Geoffrey doesn't say where it stood, and it hasn't been placed for certain.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Gorlois](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gorlois)

## Dinoot

Also: Dinoot

The abbot of the great monastery at Bangor-on-Dee, learned in the liberal arts, in Geoffrey's story and in Bede's. He tells Augustine that the British bishops owe him no obedience and won't preach to the English, their enemies.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## Diocletian

Also: Diocletiani

The Roman emperor from 284 to 305 CE, who in 303 CE began the empire's last and harshest persecution of Christians. Geoffrey says it nearly wiped out Christianity in Britain, and that Alban, Julius and Aaron died in it.

Wikipedia: [Diocletian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diocletian)

## Dionotus

Also: Dionotus, Dionotum

King of Cornwall in Geoffrey's story after his brother Caradocus. Maximianus leaves him in charge of Britain while he fights in Gaul. He's the father of Ursula, and is known only from Geoffrey.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Dionotus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dionotus)

## Diwanius

Also: Diwanio

A bishop in Geoffrey's story, given the bishop's seat of Winchester when Arthur shares out the church's offices after his crown-wearing. Geoffrey tells nothing more of him here.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## Dol

Also: Dolensis

Dol-de-Bretagne, a small town of northeast Brittany, near Mont Saint-Michel, whose cathedral is named for Saint Samson. In Geoffrey's story it's an archbishop's seat, and Chelianus is appointed to it.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Dol-de-Bretagne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dol-de-Bretagne)

## Doldavius

Also: Doldavius

The ruler of Gotland in Geoffrey's story, who hears that nobody can stand against Arthur and comes of his own accord to submit and promise him tribute. He's at Arthur's crown-wearing at the City of the Legions.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## Dorchester

Also: Dorocestrensis, Dorecestrensis

Earl Jonathal's town in Geoffrey's story. It could be Dorchester in Dorset, in southern England, the Romans' Durnovaria, or Dorchester-on-Thames, in Oxfordshire, once a bishop's seat, and Geoffrey doesn't say which.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## Dorobellum

Also: Dorobellum

The town where Cassivellaunus gathers his nobles to plan how to meet Julius Caesar's first landing. Giles's index takes it for Deal, in Kent, near where Caesar is thought to have come ashore.

## Dubricius

Also: Dubricius, Dubricio

Dyfrig in Welsh, a bishop of southeast Wales in the 500s CE, remembered as a founder of churches. Geoffrey makes him archbishop of the City of the Legions, raised to that see by Aurelius Ambrosius.

Wikipedia: [Dubricius](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dubricius)

## Dubricius of Brittany

Also: ex Dubricio rege, Dubricius, king of the Britons of Brittany

The king of the Britons of Brittany Geoffrey names as Hoel's father, who married Arthur's sister. Giles and San-Marte both print Dubricius, the archbishop's name, and San-Marte thinks Geoffrey turned Budic, the Breton king of Part 6, into Dubricius here.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## Dunvallo Molmutius

Also: Dunwallo, Dunwallonis, Dunvallo

Cloten's son in Geoffrey's story, who ends the civil war by beating the other kings, partly by dressing his men in dead enemies' armor. He's the first in Britain to wear a gold crown, and gives the Britons the Molmutine Laws. Welsh tradition calls him Dyfnwal Moelmud.

Wikipedia: [Dyfnwal Moelmud](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dyfnwal_Moelmud)

## Dyfed

Also: Demetiæ, Demetorum, Demetiorum, Demeticum, Demetici, Demeti, Demetios

The kingdom of southwest Wales, named after the Demetae, the people who lived there in Roman times. Geoffrey's Demetia stretches over south Wales, and he says its chief city was the City of the Legions.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Kingdom of Dyfed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_Dyfed)

## Eagle of Shaftesbury

Also: prophetiis Aquilæ

The eagle that spoke while the walls of Shaftesbury were being built, in Geoffrey's story of King Hudibras. Its prophecies are among the books King Alan reads to test what the angel told Cadwaladr, and they agree with it.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## Eba

Also: Eba

A leader of the Mercians who joins Wulfhere's rising against Oswiu in Geoffrey's story. Bede names him Eafa, one of three Mercian nobles who threw off Oswiu's rule and made Wulfhere king.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Eba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eba)

## Ebissa

Also: Ebissa

A Saxon leader who Hengist invites over from Germany with his son Octa, asking Vortigern to give them lands in the north of Britain. He's known only from the legend of Hengist and Horsa.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Hengist and Horsa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hengist_and_Horsa)

## Ebraucus

Also: Ebraucus, Ebrauci, Ebraucum

Mempricius's son in Geoffrey's story, a very tall, strong king who raids Gaul and founds York, Alclud and other towns. By twenty wives he has twenty sons and thirty daughters, and he sends the daughters to Italy and the sons to conquer Germany.

Wikipedia: [Ebraucus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ebraucus)

## Edadus

Also: atque Eldadus

Cherin's second son in Geoffrey's story, who reigns after his brother Fulgenius and before his brother Andragius. Geoffrey tells nothing else of him, and Giles prints him *Eldadus*.

Wikipedia: [Edadus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edadus)

## Edbert

Also: Edberto

A leader of the Mercians who joins Wulfhere's rising against Oswiu in Geoffrey's story. Bede names him Eadberht, one of three Mercian nobles who threw off Oswiu's rule and made Wulfhere king.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## Edwin

Also: Edwinus, Edwino, Edwini, Edwinum

The son of the king of Deira, who Geoffrey has raised with Cadwallon at the court of Cadfan, king of the Britons, as his foster brother. He's the real Edwin of Northumbria, king from 616 to 633 CE.

Wikipedia: [Edwin of Northumbria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edwin_of_Northumbria)

## Egypt

Also: Ægyptum, Ægypti

The land of the Nile in northeast Africa, a Roman province in the time of Claudius. Geoffrey names it as the country the apostle Peter sent Mark the Evangelist to preach in.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Egypt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Egypt)

## Eldol

Also: Eldol: cui successit

The king after Arthmail in Geoffrey's list of the kings of Britain, followed by Redon. Geoffrey tells nothing of him but his name and his place in the line.

Wikipedia: [Eldol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eldol)

## Eldol of Gloucester

Also: nomine Eldol, Eldol ducem, Eldol dux, frater Eldol

The earl of Gloucester in Geoffrey's story, the one lord to fight his way out of the massacre at Hengist's peace meeting. He snatches up a stake, kills seventy Saxons with it and escapes to his city. Welsh tradition knows him as Eidol the Mighty.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## Eledanius

Also: Eledanio

A bishop in Geoffrey's story, given the bishop's seat of Alclud when Arthur shares out the church's offices after his crown-wearing. Geoffrey tells nothing more of him here.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## Eli

Also: Heli sacerdos
