The old priest at the shrine at Shiloh, in the Bible's First Book of Samuel, who judged Israel for forty years. Geoffrey dates Brutus's founding of his city to the time when Eli ruled in Judea and the Philistines captured the Ark of the Covenant.

Wikipedia: [Eli (biblical figure)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eli_(biblical_figure))

## Elidurus

Also: Elidurum, Elidurus, Eliduro, Eliduri, the Dutiful

Morvidus's son in Geoffrey's story, made king when the lords throw out his brother Archgallo. He gives Archgallo back the crown and is called the Dutiful for it, and he reigns three times, the last after his brothers Ingenius and Peredurus have kept him in prison.

Wikipedia: [Elidurus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elidurus)

## Elijah

Also: Elias oravit

The prophet of northern Israel in the 800s BCE who fought the worship of Baal and, the Bible says, was carried up to heaven in a whirlwind. Geoffrey dates his prayer that no rain fall on the earth to King Bladud's reign.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Elijah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elijah)

## Eliud

Also: Eliud

The king after Urianus in Geoffrey's list of the kings of Britain. Geoffrey tells nothing of him but his name and his place in the line, and Cledaucus follows him.

Wikipedia: [Eliud](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eliud)

## Elsingius

Also: Elsingii

The king of Norway in Geoffrey's story, whose daughter Brennius marries to win his help against his brother Belinus. Guichtlac, king of the Danes, had loved her, and he chases Brennius's fleet to take her.

Wikipedia: [List of legendary kings of Denmark](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_legendary_kings_of_Denmark)

## Emperor Leo

Also: Leone Imperatore, emperor Leo, Leoni regi Romanorum

The emperor of Rome in Geoffrey's story, Frollo's master, who has put Frollo in charge of Gaul. Wikipedia's Lucius Tiberius says Geoffrey may mean Leo I, emperor in the east from 457 to 474 CE, but nothing settles it.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## Enniaunus

Also: Enniaunus, Enniauni

Marganus II's brother in Geoffrey's story, who chooses cruelty over justice and is thrown off the throne in the sixth year of his reign. His cousin Idvallo takes his place.

Wikipedia: [Enniaunus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enniaunus)

## Eopa

Also: Eopa

A Saxon in Geoffrey's story who has learned the Britons' language and their ways, and knows medicine. He offers to kill King Aurelius for Vortigern's son Pasgen in return for a reward, and goes to the king's court at Winchester as a monk and a doctor.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Ambrosius Aurelianus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ambrosius_Aurelianus)

## Eosa

Also: Eosa, Eosam

Hengist's relative, a Saxon leader in Geoffrey's story. After Hengist's defeat he holds Alclud against Aurelius, and he later joins Hengist's son Octa in his wars against the Britons. He's known only from Geoffrey's story.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Octa of Kent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Octa_of_Kent)

## Episford

Also: Episford

A ford where Vortimer fights the second of his battles against the Saxons, and where Horsa and Vortimer's brother Catigern kill each other. English tradition puts it at Aylesford, on the Medway in Kent.

Wikipedia: [Vortimer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vortimer)

## Ergyng

Also: Hergin

A small kingdom of the Welsh borderland west of the Wye, later called Archenfield, in today's Herefordshire. Geoffrey says Vortigern's last fort stood there, on a hill called Cloarius above the river.

Wikipedia: [Ergyng](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ergyng)

## Estrildis

Also: Estrildis, Estrildem, Estrildemque

A German king's daughter in Geoffrey's story, carried off by Humber the Hun and kept by Locrinus for her beauty. He hides her under Trinovantum for seven years, has a daughter with her and makes her queen, and Gwendolen has mother and daughter drowned in the Severn.

Wikipedia: [Estrildis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Estrildis)

## Estrusienses

Also: Estrusiensium

A people of Gaul in Geoffrey's story who send men to Arthur's war on Rome. Wikipedia's Bedivere says Geoffrey's Estrusia is Normandy, the land Arthur gives Bedivere, so they're likely the Normans.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Bedivere](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bedivere)

## Europe

Also: Europam

The continent west of Asia, which in Geoffrey's time meant the Christian kingdoms from Ireland to Greece. Geoffrey says Arvirargus's fame spread through all of it, so that Rome talked of him.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Europe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Europe)

## Eurystheus

Also: Eurystheus

The king of Tiryns and Mycenae in the Greek myths who set Hercules his twelve labors. Geoffrey makes him a king of Sparta in the days of Saul.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Eurystheus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eurystheus)

## Evander

Also: Evander, Evandro, Evandrum

The king of Syria in Geoffrey's story, an ally of Lucius Tiberius. He helps lead the ambush on the Britons taking the prisoners to Paris, kills Borellus of Le Mans with his lance, and is killed himself before the Romans scatter.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## Excalibur

Also: Caliburno, Caliburnus

Arthur's sword, which Geoffrey calls Caliburnus, the best of swords, forged on Avalon. Arthur kills four hundred seventy Saxons with it alone at Bath. Geoffrey's name is a Latin form of the Welsh Caledfwlch, and the French romances turned it into Excalibur.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Excalibur](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Excalibur)

## Exeter

Also: Kaerpen-Huelgoit, Kaerpenhuelgoit, Exonia, Exoniam

The cathedral city of Devon in southwest England, the Romans' Isca. Geoffrey gives its British name as Kaerpenhuelgoit, and has Vespasian besiege it until Arvirargus comes to fight him.

Wikipedia: [Exeter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exeter)

## Fagan

Also: Faganum

One of the two teachers Pope Eleutherius sends to baptize King Lucius in Geoffrey's story, with Deruvian. Welsh churches honor him as a saint, and St Fagans near Cardiff bears his name.

Wikipedia: [Fagan (saint)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fagan_(saint))

## Ferrex

Also: Ferrex, Ferrecem

Gorboduc's son in Geoffrey's story, who escapes his brother Porrex's plot to kill him and comes back from Gaul with an army of Franks. He's killed in battle with all his men, and his mother takes revenge.

Wikipedia: [Ferrex](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferrex)

## Flanders

Also: Flandrias

The Dutch-speaking north of Belgium, and in the Middle Ages a county along the North Sea reaching into France. In Geoffrey's story Holdinus, ruler of the Ruteni, is carried there after the great battle to be buried.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Flanders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flanders)

## Forest of Dean

Also: Daneium nemus

An old forest in western Gloucestershire, England, between the rivers Severn and Wye, long a royal hunting forest. In Merlin's prophecy it wakes and cries out in a human voice to Wales and Winchester.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Forest of Dean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Forest_of_Dean)

## Franks

Also: Francorum, Franci

A Germanic people of the lower Rhine who conquered Roman Gaul in the 400s and 500s CE, giving France its name. Geoffrey makes them a kingdom already in King Leir's day, when Leir's daughter marries their king Aganippus.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Franks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Franks)

## Frigg

Also: Fream

The goddess Hengist names as the most powerful his people worship, after Woden. In the old Germanic myths she was Woden's wife, and Friday is named after her.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Frigg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frigg)

## Frollo

Also: Flolloni, Flollo, Flollonis, Flollonem

The Roman tribune who rules Gaul for the emperor Leo in Geoffrey's story. Beaten by Arthur, he shuts himself in Paris, and when his people begin to starve he challenges Arthur to fight him alone for the kingdom.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Lucius Tiberius](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lucius_Tiberius)

## Fulgenius

Also: Fulgenius videlicet

Cherin's oldest son in Geoffrey's story, the first of three brothers to reign one after another. Geoffrey tells nothing else of him, and his brother Edadus succeeds him.

Wikipedia: [Fulgenius](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fulgenius)

## Fulgenius the rebel

Also: duce Fulgenio, Fulgenium, cum Fulgenio, dux Fulgenius

The leader of the Britons who fight Severus in Geoffrey's story, and the brother of Bassianus's British mother. He shares his name with the earlier King Fulgenius, Cherin's son, and is known only from Geoffrey.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## Gabias

Also: Gabius, Gabii, Gabio

One of the two consuls governing Rome in Geoffrey's story when Belinus and Brennius march on it. He buys peace, breaks it to help the Germans, and is killed when the brothers take the city. Rome never had a consul of that name, and Giles prints him *Gabius*.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Belinus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Belinus)

## Gad the prophet

Also: et Gad

A prophet at King David's court in the Bible, who brought David Yahweh's word. Geoffrey names him with Nathan and Asaph as prophets in Israel when King Ebraucus reigned in Britain.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Gad (prophet)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gad_(prophet))

## Gaius Metellus Cotta

Also: Caius Metellus Cotta, Caium Metellum

A Roman senator in Geoffrey's story who marches with Lucius Tiberius against Arthur. In the great battle he helps lead a wedge of the front line with Boccus, king of the Medes.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## Gaius Quintilianus

Also: Caius Quintilianus, Quintilianum

The nephew of Lucius Tiberius in Geoffrey's story. When Arthur's envoys order Lucius out of Gaul, he sneers that the Britons are better at boasting than fighting, and Gawain cuts off his head, which starts the war.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Lucius Tiberius](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lucius_Tiberius)

## Galabes

Also: Galabes

A place Geoffrey names twice. In Merlin's prophecy it's a valley a heron raises into a high mountain to build its nest on, and later it's the spring in the land of the Gewisse where Aurelius's messengers find Merlin, who often went there. Geoffrey doesn't say where it is, and no one has placed it for certain.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## Galluc

Also: Galluc

An earl of Salisbury in Geoffrey's story, one of the earls of the great cities who come to Arthur's crown-wearing in the City of the Legions. Geoffrey names Anaraut as earl of Salisbury too, in the same list.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## Gascony

Also: Guasconiam

A region of southwest France, between the river Garonne and the Pyrenees, named after the Vascones, the Basques. In Geoffrey's story Hoel lays it waste with fire and sword and brings its princes under him.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Gascony](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gascony)

## Gaul

Also: Galliam, Gallias, Gallia, Galliæ, Galliarum, Galliis, Gallicana, Gallicanum, Gallicanos, Gallicanæ, Gallicanam, Gallorumque

The Roman land west of the Rhine, roughly today's France and Belgium, across the Channel from Britain. Geoffrey sets Britain between it and Ireland in his opening description, and says twelve kings ruled it together when Brutus came. It's the land the history's Britons cross to most often, in war and in flight.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Gaul](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gaul)

## Gauls

Also: Galli, Gallorum, Gallis, Gallos

The Celtic peoples of Gaul, today's France and Belgium, before and under Roman rule. In Geoffrey's story their twelve kings take in Goffarius when Brutus drives him out of Aquitaine, and their army besieges the Trojans near the place where Tours now stands.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Gauls](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gauls)

## Gawain

Also: Walgannum, Walvanus, Walganius, Walganio, Walganium, Walguainus, Walgainus, Walgaino, Walgainum

The son of Lot and Arthur's sister, Arthur's nephew, who, Geoffrey says, was sent at twelve to be raised in the household of Pope Sulpicius. He's Gawain, the most famous of Arthur's knights in the later romances.

Wikipedia: [Gawain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gawain)

## Gemini

Also: Gemini

The twins, the third sign of the zodiac, drawn as two brothers with their arms around each other, the twins Castor and Pollux of Greek myth. In Merlin's prophecy they give up their usual embrace.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Gemini (astrology)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gemini_(astrology))

## Genoreu

Also: Genoreu

The fort where Vortigern takes refuge in Geoffrey's story, in the land of Ergyng above the river Wye, on a hill called Cloarius. Giles's index calls it a village on the Wye, and Wikipedia's Ambrosius Aurelianus places it at the hill fort of Little Doward, in Herefordshire, England.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Ambrosius Aurelianus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ambrosius_Aurelianus)

## Geoffrey of Monmouth

Also: Galfredi Monumetensis, Galfridus, Gaufridus, Gaufridus Monumetensis

A Welsh or Breton cleric of the 1100s CE, a teacher at Oxford and later bishop of St Asaph, who wrote this history about 1136. He names himself in his dedication, and his book made Arthur famous across Europe.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Geoffrey of Monmouth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geoffrey_of_Monmouth)

## Gerennus

Also: Geruntius

Elidurus's son in Geoffrey's story, who succeeds Runo as king of Britain. Geoffrey gives only his name and his place in the line, and Giles prints him *Geruntius*.

Wikipedia: [Gerennus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gerennus)

## Gerion

Also: Gerionem

The augur, a reader of omens, who Brutus takes to Diana's temple with twelve older men to ask where his people should settle. He's known only from Geoffrey's story.

## Germanus of Auxerre

Also: Germanus Altisiodorensis, sancto Germano

Bishop of Auxerre, in Gaul, who came to Britain with Lupus of Troyes to preach against the Pelagian heresy. In Geoffrey's story he comes in Vortigern's time and restores the true faith among the Britons.

Wikipedia: [Germanus of Auxerre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Germanus_of_Auxerre)

## Germany

Also: Germania, Germaniam, Germaniæ, Germanicus

The lands east of the Rhine, Germania to the Romans, home of the Germanic peoples. Geoffrey says King Ebraucus's sons sailed there and conquered it, and the Saxons later come from it.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Germania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Germania)

## Geta son of Severus

Also: Geta, Getam

Severus's younger son, Roman emperor with his brother from 209 CE until his brother had him murdered in 211. In Geoffrey's story the Romans make him king because his mother was Roman, and the Britons choose his brother instead.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## Gewisse

Also: Wisseorum, Gewisseorum

An Anglo-Saxon people of the upper Thames valley, the ancestors of the West Saxon kings, known from the 500s CE on. Geoffrey makes Octavius their duke long before there were any English in Britain.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Gewisse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gewisse)

## Giants' Dance

Also: chorea gigantum, choream gigantum, gigantum choream

Geoffrey's name for Stonehenge, the great ring of standing stones on Salisbury Plain in Wiltshire, England. In his story giants brought its healing stones from Africa to Mount Killaraus in Ireland, and Merlin is sent to bring them to Britain, to stand over the lords Hengist murdered.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Stonehenge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stonehenge)

## Gibeonites

Also: Gibeonitæ

A people of Canaan in the book of Joshua. When Joshua was conquering the land, they tricked him into a peace treaty by pretending to live far away, and Israel kept the oath even after the trick came out. Bishop Eldad holds them up to Aurelius as people shown mercy.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Gibeon (ancient city)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gibeon_(ancient_city))

## Gildas

Also: Gildas

A British monk of the 500s CE whose book *On the Ruin of Britain* is the only account of his century by someone who lived through it. Geoffrey names him with Bede as the historians who said nothing of Britain's kings before Christ, nor of Arthur. He also says Gildas told at length of the quarrel between King Lud and his brother Nennius, which no surviving book of Gildas tells.

Wikipedia: [Gildas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gildas)

## Gillomanius

Also: Gillomanius, Gillomanium, Gillomanio

A young king of Ireland in Geoffrey's story, known for his courage. He leads the Irish against Uther when the Britons come to take the stones of the Giants' Dance from Mount Killaraus, and later takes in Vortigern's son Pasgen.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Mount Killaraus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Killaraus)

## Glamorgan

Also: Glamorgantia

The coastal region of south Wales from Cardiff west to Swansea. Geoffrey places the City of the Legions on the Usk in Glamorgan, though Caerleon stands just east of it, in Gwent.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Glamorgan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glamorgan)

## Gloius

Also: Gloio

A son of Claudius in Geoffrey's story, born in Britain, who rules Dyfed after Arvirargus. Some say Gloucester takes its name from him. He's known only from Geoffrey.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [List of kings in Wales from the Matter of Britain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_kings_in_Wales_from_the_Matter_of_Britain)

## Gloucester

Also: Claudiocestriæ, Claudiocestria, Kaerglou, Gloucestria, Claudio-cestriæ, Claudiocestrensis, Glouecestrensis

The city on the Severn in western England, Glevum to the Romans. Geoffrey first names it in Robert of Gloucester's title, and later says the emperor Claudius founded it and it was named after him.

Wikipedia: [Gloucester](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gloucester)

## Godbold

Also: Godboldo

The king of Orkney in Geoffrey's story, who comes to help Edwin against Cadwallon and is killed with him at Heavenfield. He's known from this one passage, and no other source names him.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## Goffar the Pict

Also: Goffarius Pictus, Goffario, Goffarium, Goffarii

The king of Aquitaine and lord of the Poitevins when the Trojans come ashore there. He sends envoys to ask whether they come for peace or war, and when they kill one he raises an army against them.

Wikipedia: [Goffar the Pict](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goffar_the_Pict)

## Gogmagog

Also: Goëmagot

A loathsome giant about 18 feet tall who could pull an oak from the ground like a hazel switch. Geoffrey calls him Goemagot; he attacks Brutus's people with twenty other giants, and Brutus keeps him alive to wrestle Corineus.

Wikipedia: [Gogmagog (giant)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gogmagog_(giant))

## Gombertus

Also: Gomberto

In Geoffrey's story, the Norwegian king Octavius sails to for help after Trahern drives him from his throne. Geoffrey tells nothing more of him, and he's known only from this passage.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## Goneril

Also: Gonorilla, Gonorillæ

Leir's oldest daughter in Geoffrey's story, who swears she loves him more than her own soul and is married to Maglaurus of Albany with a third of Britain. Later she cuts her father's knights from sixty to thirty, then to one.

Wikipedia: [Goneril](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goneril)

## Gorboduc

Also: Gorbogudo

A king in Geoffrey's story, the father of Ferrex and Porrex, whose quarrel over who'll succeed him ends in both their deaths and years of civil war. Giles prints his name *Gorbogudo*.

Wikipedia: [Gorboduc](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gorboduc)

## Gorbonianus

Also: Gorbonianus, Gorbonianum, Gorboniani

Morvidus's oldest son in Geoffrey's story, the most just king of his time, who honors the gods first, rebuilds their temples and protects the farmers from their lords. His brothers Archgallo, Elidurus, Ingenius and Peredurus reign after him.

Wikipedia: [Gorbonianus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gorbonianus)

## Gorlois

Also: Gorlois, Gorloi

The duke of Cornwall in Geoffrey's story and the husband of Igraine, a man of good judgment and ripe age. He fights beside Aurelius against Hengist and advises Uther in his war with the Saxons. When Uther falls in love with Igraine, Gorlois leaves the court in anger.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Gorlois](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gorlois)

## Gormund

Also: Gormundum, Gormondum

A king of the Africans in Geoffrey's story, who conquers Ireland and crosses to Britain at the Saxons' call. He burns Cirencester and the island from sea to sea, and gives Loegria to the Saxons. He comes from the Old French poem Gormont et Isembart.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## Gotland

Also: Gothlandiæ, Godlandiæ, Godlandiam

The largest island of the Baltic Sea, part of Sweden. In Geoffrey's story its king, Doldavius, submits to Arthur of his own accord and promises tribute.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Gotland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gotland)

## Gracianus Municeps

Also: Gratianum Municipem, Gratianus Municeps

A soldier in Geoffrey's story, sent by Maximianus with two legions to drive the Picts and Huns out of Britain. His byname means a citizen of a free town, and historians take him from Gratian, made emperor by Rome's army in Britain in 406 CE.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Gracianus Municeps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gracianus_Municeps)

## Gratian

Also: Gratiani, Gratianum, Gratianus

A Roman emperor of the west from 367 to 383 CE, with his brother Valentinian. In Geoffrey's story the two refuse Maximianus a third of the empire, and Gratian later sends the Huns and Picts against Maximianus's supporters.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Gratian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gratian)

## Greece

Also: Græciam, Græcia, Græciæ

The land of the Greeks, at the southeast end of Europe. Geoffrey's Greece is ruled by King Pandrasus, who holds the descendants of the captured Trojans as slaves.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Greece](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greece)

## Greeks

Also: Græcorum, Græcos, Græcus, Græci, Græco, Græcis, Græcum

The people of Greece, who in Homer's story besieged and burned Troy. In Geoffrey's legend they still hold the Trojans' descendants as slaves generations later, until Brutus leads them out.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Greeks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greeks)

## Gregory the Great

Also: Gregorio

Pope from 590 to 604 CE, a Roman noble turned monk and one of the great teachers of the Western Church. Geoffrey names him as the blessed pope who sent Augustine to Britain to preach to the English.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Pope Gregory I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pope_Gregory_I)

## Guales

Also: Guales

A queen of the Britons who, Geoffrey says, may have given the Welsh their name. She's Geoffrey's own, made to explain the word, which really comes from the Old English for "foreigner."<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## Gualo

Also: Gualone

A leader of the Britons who, Geoffrey says, may have given the Welsh their name. He's Geoffrey's own, made to explain the word, which really comes from the Old English for "foreigner."<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## Guerinus

Also: Guerinus, Guerino, Guerinum

The earl of Chartres in Geoffrey's story, who leads the twelve peers of Gaul to Arthur's crown-wearing in the City of the Legions. Geoffrey tells nothing more of him here.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## Guernsey

Also: Garnareia

An island in the English Channel off the coast of Normandy, one of the Channel Islands. In Geoffrey's story a storm drives Cadwallon's ship there, and Brian feeds the sick king there with flesh cut from his own thigh.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Guernsey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guernsey)

## Guerthaeth

Also: Guerthaeth

One of the three kings under Cassivellaunus in Geoffrey's story who urge him to attack Julius Caesar's camp at once. Geoffrey makes him king of Gwynedd. He's known only from Geoffrey.

Wikipedia: [List of kings in Wales from the Matter of Britain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_kings_in_Wales_from_the_Matter_of_Britain)

## Guichtlac

Also: Guichthlacus, Guichthlaci

The king of the Danes in Geoffrey's story, who loves the Norwegian king's daughter and chases her husband Brennius's fleet to take her. A storm drives him ashore in Northumbria, where he's caught and brought to Belinus with her. Giles prints him *Guichthlacus*.

Wikipedia: [List of legendary kings of Denmark](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_legendary_kings_of_Denmark)

## Guiderius

Also: Guiderius, Guiderio

Kymbelinus's older son in Geoffrey's story, who refuses Rome its tribute and so brings Claudius's invasion. Hamo, disguised in British armor, kills him in the battle, and his brother Arvirargus takes his place.

Wikipedia: [Guiderius](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guiderius)

## Guillamurius

Also: Guillamurius

The king of Ireland in Geoffrey's story, who sails to help the Scots and Picts while Arthur besieges them on Loch Lomond. Arthur drives his army home, and later lands in Ireland to bring it under him.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## Guinevere

Also: Guanhumaram, Ganhumaræ, Ganhumaram

Arthur's queen, born of a noble Roman family and raised in the household of Cador, duke of Cornwall, the most beautiful woman in Britain. Geoffrey calls her Guanhumara; the later legend knows her as Guinevere.

Wikipedia: [Guinevere](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guinevere)

## Guitardus

Also: Guitardum, Guitardumque, Guitardus

The duke of the Poitevins in Geoffrey's story. Arthur sends Hoel against him after Frollo's death, and Hoel wears him down in many battles until he surrenders; he comes to Arthur's crown-wearing as Guitardus of Poitou.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## Guithelin

Also: Guithelinus diadema, ut Guithelinus

Gurguit Barbtruc's successor in Geoffrey's story, a king who rules kindly and modestly all his life. His wife Marcia writes the Marcian law, and when he dies she rules for their young son Sisillius II.

Wikipedia: [Guithelin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guithelin)

## Gunvasius

Also: Gunfasius, Gunvasius

The king of Orkney in Geoffrey's story, who comes of his own accord to submit to Arthur and promise him tribute once Ireland and Iceland are his. Giles prints his name Gunfasius at his first appearance and Gunvasius after.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## Guoyrancgonus

Also: Gorangano

The lord of Kent when Hengist's Saxons come to Britain, who Geoffrey calls Gorangonus. Vortigern gives Kent to Hengist without his knowledge, as the price of Hengist's daughter.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## Gurgintius

Also: Gurgintius

The king after Clotenus in Geoffrey's list of the kings of Britain. Geoffrey tells nothing of him but his name and his place in the line, and Merianus follows him.

Wikipedia: [Gurgintius](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gurgintius)

## Gurguit Barbtruc

Also: Gurgiunt, Brabtruc, Gurguit

Belinus's son and heir in Geoffrey's story, a modest, sensible king who brings rebel neighbors back under his rule and conquers Denmark again when its king stops paying tribute. Sailing home, he meets Partholón's exiles and gives them Ireland. Giles prints him *Gurgiunt Brabtruc*.

Wikipedia: [Gurguit Barbtruc](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gurguit_Barbtruc)

## Gurgustius

Also: Gurgustius, Gurgustii

Rivallo's son in Geoffrey's story, the first of the kings he lists between Rivallo and Gorboduc with nothing told of them but their names. His nephew Jago reigns after Sisillius.

Wikipedia: [Gurgustius](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gurgustius)

## Gwendolen

Also: Guendolænam, Guendolœna, Guendolœnam

Corineus's daughter and Locrinus's wife in Geoffrey's story. When Locrinus leaves her for Estrildis, she raises Cornwall against him and he's killed in the battle. She drowns Estrildis and her daughter, and rules Britain for fifteen years for her son Maddan.

Wikipedia: [Queen Gwendolen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Queen_Gwendolen)

## Gwynedd

Also: Venedociæ, Venedoti, Venedotos, Venedotorum, Venedocia

The kingdom of northwest Wales, its heartland the mountains of Snowdonia and the island of Anglesey. Geoffrey calls it Venedotia and says its people are now called the North Welsh.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Kingdom of Gwynedd](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_Gwynedd)

## Hafren

Also: Sabren

The daughter of Locrinus and Estrildis in Geoffrey's story. Gwendolen has her thrown into the Severn with her mother, and Geoffrey says the river was named after her, Hafren in Welsh and Sabrina in Latin.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Hafren](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hafren)

## Haggai

Also: Aggeus

A Jewish prophet of the 500s BCE, after the exile in Babylon, who urged the people to rebuild Yahweh's temple. Geoffrey names him with Amos and Azariah among the prophets of the time of an early British king, centuries before Haggai lived.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Haggai](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haggai)

## Hamo

Also: Hamonis, Hamo, Levis hamo

A Roman commander in Geoffrey's story who comes to Britain with the emperor Claudius. Geoffrey names Southampton Hamo's Port after him when Belinus's road runs there, long before his time, as Giles's index says.

Wikipedia: [Guiderius](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guiderius)

## Heavenfield

Also: Hevenfeld

A field near Hexham, in Northumberland, by Hadrian's Wall, where Oswald of Northumbria beat Cadwallon in 634 CE, Bede says. Geoffrey sets Edwin's battle against the Britons there instead.

Wikipedia: [Battle of Heavenfield](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Heavenfield)

## Hector

Also: Hectoris

The oldest son of King Priam and the greatest of the Trojan warriors in Homer's *Iliad*, killed by Achilles. Geoffrey says Hector's sons ruled in Troy when Brutus founded his city, having driven out Antenor's descendants.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Hector](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hector)

## Helena

Also: Helena, Helenam, Helenæ

The mother of Constantine the Great, a Christian saint who in old age went to Jerusalem, where legend says she found Christ's cross. Geoffrey makes her the daughter of King Coel, taught to rule, and the wife of Constantius.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Helena, mother of Constantine I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helena,_mother_of_Constantine_I)

## Helena niece of Hoel

Also: Helenam neptem

Hoel's niece in Geoffrey's story, another woman than Constantine's mother. A giant from Spain carries her and her nurse off to Mont Saint-Michel, and she dies of fear in his arms. Hoel builds a church over her grave.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## Helena's Tomb

Also: Tumba Helenæ

Geoffrey's name for the smaller rock near Mont Saint-Michel where Hoel builds a church over his niece Helena's grave. It's the islet of Tombelaine, whose name one folk story explains as the tomb of Hélène.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Tombelaine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tombelaine)

## Helenus

Also: Heleni, Helenum

A son of King Priam of Troy and a seer, carried off to Greece as a captive after Troy fell. Geoffrey says Brutus found Helenus's descendants held as slaves by Pandrasus, king of the Greeks.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Helenus (son of Priam)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helenus_(son_of_Priam))

## Heli

Also: Heli filius ejus

Digueillus's son in Geoffrey's story, who rules forty years and fathers Lud, Cassivellaunus and Nennius. Welsh tradition knows him as Beli Mawr, Beli the Great, the ancestor of many royal lines.

Wikipedia: [Beli Mawr](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beli_Mawr)

## Hengist

Also: Hengistus, Hengisto, Hengisti, Hengistum

The leader of the Saxons who come ashore in Kent with his brother Horsa in three long ships, exiles from Germany, in Vortigern's time. Vortigern takes them into his service against the Picts, and Hengist becomes the Britons' great enemy.

Wikipedia: [Hengist and Horsa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hengist_and_Horsa)

## Henry I

Also: Henricus, Henricum

King of England from 1100 to 1135 CE, the youngest son of William the Conqueror. Geoffrey praises Robert of Gloucester as Henry's son, saying Britain rejoiced in Robert as in a second Henry.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Henry I of England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_I_of_England)

## Henry of Huntingdon

Also: Henrico Huntingdonensi

An archdeacon of Huntingdon and the author of the History of the English, written in the 1130s CE. Geoffrey leaves the Saxon kings to him, and tells him to say nothing of the British ones.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Henry of Huntingdon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_of_Huntingdon)

## Henwinus

Also: Hernuinum, Henuino, Henuinus

Regan's husband and Cunedagius's father in Geoffrey's story. He's a duke, and rises with Maglaurus against Leir and takes his kingdom. Giles prints his name *Hernuinus* and *Henuinus*.

Wikipedia: [Leir of Britain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leir_of_Britain)

## Hider

Also: Hiderus, Hider

A Briton in Geoffrey's story who brings five thousand men to help the Britons when Petreius drives them back into the wood. His son is one of the four nobles killed in the Roman ambush.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## Hirelgas

Also: Hirelgas

Bedivere's nephew in Geoffrey's story. When Boccus kills Bedivere in the great battle, he rides through the enemy with three hundred men, kills the king, and tears his body apart beside his uncle's, then rallies the Britons.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## Hirelgas of Periron

Also: Hirelgam Deperirum

One of four British nobles in Geoffrey's story killed in the Roman ambush on the escort taking the prisoners to Paris. He's another man than Hirelgas, Bedivere's nephew, who fights in the great battle.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## Hirelglas

Also: Hirelglas

Cassivellaunus's nephew in Geoffrey's story, killed by Androgeus's nephew Cuelinus after a wrestling match at the feast for the victory over Caesar. His death drives Androgeus to call Caesar back to Britain.

Wikipedia: [Mandubracius](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mandubracius)

## Hirtacius

Also: Hirtacius, Hirtacium

The king of the Parthians in Geoffrey's story, who brings his army to Lucius Tiberius against Arthur. In the great battle he leads a wedge with the senator Marius Lepidus against Aschillius, king of the Danes.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## Hoel

Also: Hoelum, Hoelus, Hoelo, Hoeli

The king of the Britons of Brittany in Geoffrey's story, Arthur's nephew, the son of Arthur's sister. He crosses with fifteen thousand men to help Arthur against the Saxons, and fights at his side from then on. Wikipedia's Hywel the Great takes him for a Breton king of the late fifth century CE.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Hywel the Great](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hywel_the_Great)

## Holdinus

Also: Holdinus

The king of the Ruteni, a people of southern Gaul, in Geoffrey's story, first of the lords from overseas at Arthur's crown-wearing in the City of the Legions. Geoffrey tells nothing more of him here.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## Homer

Also: Homerus

The Greek poet of the *Iliad* and the *Odyssey*, the oldest poems of Europe. Geoffrey claims Homer says Brutus later built Tours, though nothing of the kind is in Homer.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Homer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homer)

## Horsa

Also: Horsus, Horsum

Hengist's brother, who lands with him in Kent leading the first Saxons to come to Britain in Vortigern's time. English tradition remembers the two brothers as the founders of the kingdom of Kent.

Wikipedia: [Hengist and Horsa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hengist_and_Horsa)

## Hosea

Also: Osee

A prophet of northern Israel in the 700s BCE, who compared Israel's worship of other gods to a wife cheating on her husband. Geoffrey dates him with Isaiah to the reign of an early British king, when Rome was founded.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Hosea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hosea)

## Hudibras

Also: Hudibras

Leil's son in Geoffrey's story, who ends the civil war his father left and reigns thirty-nine years. He founds Canterbury, Winchester and Shaftesbury, and Wikipedia names him Rud Hud Hudibras.

Wikipedia: [Rud Hud Hudibras](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rud_Hud_Hudibras)

## Humber

Also: Humbræ, vocatur Humber, trans Humbrum, Humbro, Humbri, citra Humbrum, Humbrum

The wide tidal estuary of eastern England between Yorkshire and Lincolnshire, where the Ouse and the Trent meet the sea. Geoffrey names it with the Thames and the Severn as one of Britain's three great rivers, along which ships bring trade from every nation.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Humber](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Humber)

## Humber the Hun

Also: Humber rex, Humbrum in fugam, prædictus Humber

A king of the Huns in Geoffrey's story who lands in Albany and kills Brutus's son Albanactus. Beaten by Locrinus and Camber, he drowns as he flees in the river that Geoffrey says still bears his name, the Humber.

Wikipedia: [Humber the Hun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Humber_the_Hun)

## Huns

Also: Hunnorum

A nomadic people from the steppes of Central Asia who reached Europe in the 370s CE and, under Attila, raided the Roman Empire. Geoffrey makes Humber, the invader Locrinus beats, a king of the Huns, many centuries before there were any.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Huns](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Huns)

## Iceland

Also: Islandiam, Islandiæ

The island country of the north Atlantic, settled by the Norse only in the 870s CE. In Geoffrey's story Arthur sails there after taking Ireland, beats its people and brings it under him.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Iceland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iceland)

## Idvallo

Also: Idvallo

Ingenius's son in Geoffrey's story, put on the throne in place of his cousin Enniaunus. Taught by Enniaunus's fall, he cares for right and fairness, and Runo succeeds him.

Wikipedia: [Idvallo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Idvallo)

## Igraine

Also: Igerna, Igernam, Igernæ

The wife of Gorlois, duke of Cornwall, the most beautiful woman in Britain. King Uther falls in love with her at his Easter feast in London.

Wikipedia: [Igraine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Igraine)

## Imbertus

Also: Imbertum, Imbertus

One of Goffar's envoys, who shoots an arrow at the Trojan Corineus for hunting in the king's forest without permission. He's known only from Geoffrey's story.

Wikipedia: [Goffar the Pict](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goffar_the_Pict)

## Inbaltus

Also: Inbaltus, Inbalto

The leader of the Gauls of Armorica in Geoffrey's story, who meets Maximianus's army when it lands and falls with fifteen thousand of his men. He's known only from this passage.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## Ingenius

Also: Vigenius et Peredurus, cecidit Vigenio, obiit Vigenius, Vigenii filius

Morvidus's son in Geoffrey's story, who with his brother Peredurus overthrows and imprisons their brother Elidurus. He rules the land west of the Humber for seven years, and Giles prints his name *Vigenius*.

Wikipedia: [Ingenius of Britain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ingenius_of_Britain)

## Ini

Also: Ini

Cadwaladr's nephew in Geoffrey's story, who goes back to Britain with Ivor and fights the English for forty-nine years. His name recalls Ine, king of the West Saxons, who also gave up his crown and died in Rome.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Ine of Wessex](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ine_of_Wessex)

## Innogen

Also: Ignogen, Ignoge

Pandrasus's oldest daughter, who the Trojans demand as Brutus's wife as the price of the king's freedom. Geoffrey calls her Ignoge; later English writers spelled her name Innogen.

Wikipedia: [Innogen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Innogen)

## Ireland

Also: Hiberniam, Hibernia, Hiberniæ, Hibernie

The large island west of Great Britain, across the Irish Sea, which Rome never ruled. Geoffrey sets Britain between it and Gaul in his opening description. Its kings and armies come into his history again and again, as allies and as enemies of the Britons.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Ireland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ireland)

## Irish

Also: Hibernensibus, Hiberniensibusque, Hibernienses, Hibernenses

The people of Ireland. Geoffrey says the Picts, turned down by the Britons, found their wives among the Irish, and that the Scots come from the Picts and the Irish together.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Irish people](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Irish_people)

## Irish Sea

Also: Hibernicum mare

The sea between Great Britain and Ireland, joined to the Atlantic in the north and the south by narrow channels. In Geoffrey's story one of the rays of the dragon star over Winchester bends toward it.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Irish Sea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Irish_Sea)

## Isaiah

Also: Esaias

A prophet of Judah in the 700s BCE, whose warnings and promises fill the Bible's longest book of prophecy. Geoffrey dates him with Hosea to the reign of an early British king, when Rome was founded.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Isaiah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isaiah)

## Isembard

Also: Isembardus

The nephew of Louis, king of the Franks, in Geoffrey's story. Driven out of Gaul, he joins Gormund at Cirencester and gives up his Christian faith for Gormund's help against his uncle. He's the traitor of the Old French poem Gormont et Isembart.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Isembard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isembard)

## Israel

Also: in Israel

The land and people of the Bible's twelve tribes, ruled from Jerusalem by Saul, David and Solomon. Geoffrey names it where he dates his British kings by its prophets.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Kingdom of Israel (united monarchy)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_Israel_(united_monarchy))

## Israelites

Also: filios Israel

The people of Israel in the Bible, the descendants of Jacob's twelve sons. They came out of slavery in Egypt and conquered Canaan, the land Yahweh had promised them. Bishop Eldad recalls how they spared the Gibeonites.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Israelites](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israelites)

## Italy

Also: Italiam, Italiæ, Italia

The Italian peninsula, the heart of the Roman Empire. In Geoffrey's story Aeneas sails there after the fall of Troy and wins its kingdom from Turnus, and Brutus, his great-grandson, is driven out of it for killing his father.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Italy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Italy)

## Iturea

Also: Itureorum

A land of the ancient Near East, north of Galilee, from Mount Lebanon across the plain to the east. In Geoffrey's story its king, Serses, marches with Lucius Tiberius against Arthur.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Iturea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iturea)

## Ivor

Also: Ivor

Cadwaladr's son in Geoffrey's story. With his cousin Ini he sails back to Britain to rule the Britons who are left, and fights the English for forty-nine years without winning back the island.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Ivor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ivor)

## Jago

Also: Lago

A king in Geoffrey's list, Gurgustius's nephew, who reigns after Sisillius. Nothing is told of him but his name, which Giles prints *Lago* and Wikipedia gives as Jago.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Jago of Britain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jago_of_Britain)

## Janus

Also: Jani

The Roman god of doorways, gates and beginnings, shown with two faces looking both ways, and January is named after him. Geoffrey says Cordelia buried Leir in a chamber built in his honor under the Soar.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Janus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Janus)

## Jerusalem

Also: Hierusalem

The holy city of the Jews, in the hills of Judea, where King Solomon built Yahweh's temple. Geoffrey dates the temple's building to the reign of the British king who founded Carlisle.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Jerusalem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jerusalem)

## Jesus Christ

Also: Christi, Christus, Christum, Christo, Jesus, Christumque, Christ

Jesus of Nazareth, who Christians hold to be the son of Yahweh, who died on the cross and rose again. Geoffrey dates his history from Christ's birth, the incarnation, setting the kings of Britain before it and Arthur after it.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Jesus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jesus)

## Joel

Also: Joel

One of the twelve minor prophets of the Bible, whose short book tells of a plague of locusts and calls the people to turn back to their god. Geoffrey names him among the prophets of Hudibras's time.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Joel (prophet)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joel_(prophet))

## Jonathal

Also: Jonathal

The earl of Dorchester in Geoffrey's story, one of the earls of the great cities who come to Arthur's crown-wearing in the City of the Legions. Geoffrey tells nothing more of him here.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## Jordan of Tintagel

Also: Jordanum

A close friend of Gorlois, duke of Cornwall, in Geoffrey's story, from Tintagel. Merlin gives Uther's friend Ulfin the shape of Jordan on the night Uther goes into Tintagel looking like Gorlois.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## Judea

Also: Judæa

The land of the Jews around Jerusalem, in the hills west of the Dead Sea. Geoffrey dates the kings of Britain against its priests and kings, beginning with Eli, who ruled there when Brutus founded his city.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Judea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Judea)

## Judon

Also: Widen

Gorboduc's wife and the mother of Ferrex and Porrex in Geoffrey's story. Mad with grief when Porrex kills Ferrex, she and her maids kill Porrex in his sleep. Giles prints her name *Widen*.

Wikipedia: [Gorboduc](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gorboduc)

## Jugein

Also: Jugein, Vigenis

The earl of Leicester in Geoffrey's story, one of the earls of the great cities who come to Arthur's crown-wearing in the City of the Legions. Geoffrey tells nothing more of him here.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## Julius and Aaron

Also: Julius quoque et Aaron, Julii martyris, Aaron, the martyr Julius, the holy Aaron

Two Christian citizens of the City of the Legions, put to death for their faith in Diocletian's persecution. Geoffrey names them with Alban as the martyrs of that persecution in Britain.

Wikipedia: [Julius and Aaron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julius_and_Aaron)

## Julius Caesar

Also: Julio Cæsare, Cæsar, Cæsare, Cæsarem, Cæsari, Cæsaris, Julium, Julii, Caio Julio Cæsari, Caius Julius Cæsar, Julius, Julio, Caius Julius, Gaius Julius

The Roman general who conquered Gaul and crossed to Britain twice, in 55 and 54 BCE, then made himself master of Rome and was stabbed to death in 44 BCE. Geoffrey first names him as the man King Cassibellaunus, Lud's brother, fought.

Wikipedia: [Julius Caesar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julius_Caesar)

## Jupiter

Also: Jovi, Jovem, Jupiter

The chief god of the Romans, god of the sky and thunder, Zeus to the Greeks. At Diana's temple on Leogecia, Brutus and his men raise altars to three gods, Jupiter, Mercury and Diana.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Jupiter (god)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jupiter_(god))

## Juvenal

Also: Juvenalis

A Roman poet of the early 100s CE whose *Satires* mock the Rome of his day. Geoffrey quotes his fourth satire, where a flatterer hopes Arviragus will fall from his chariot.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Juvenal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Juvenal)

## Kaercorrei

Also: Kaercorrei, Thancastre

The castle Hengist builds on ground he rings with one long strap cut from a bull's hide. Geoffrey says the Britons called it Kaercorrei and the English Thancastre, both meaning the castle of the strap. It's usually taken for Caistor, in Lincolnshire, though no identification is secure.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Hengist and Horsa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hengist_and_Horsa)

## Kaerdubalum

Also: Kaerdubali

A town Merlin's prophecy names, whose fox avenges a lion and eats a bull. Geoffrey gives it a British name, as he does many towns, but no one has placed it for certain.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## Kaicester

Also: Kaicestria, Caicestria, Caicestrensis

The town of Earl Cursalem in Geoffrey's story. Giles's index takes it for Chichester, in West Sussex, "probably", while San-Marte notes the Welsh Brut Tysilio has Caer Gynvarch, and nothing settles it.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## Karitia

Also: Karitiam

A city in Gaul where, in Geoffrey's story, Cordelia lives with Aganippus and her father comes to her. Giles's index suggests Calais, but nobody knows for sure which town Geoffrey meant.

## Kay

Also: Caioque, Caius dapifer, Caio dapifero, Caius autem dapifer, Caii consulis, Cheudo

Arthur's steward in Geoffrey's story, the officer who served the king's table, a great office at a royal court. When Gaul is won, Arthur gives him Anjou. He's the Cei of the Welsh tales, one of Arthur's first companions.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Sir Kay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sir_Kay)

## Kent

Also: Cantiæ, Cantia, Cantuaritis, Cantiorum

The kingdom in the southeast corner of Britain, the nearest to Gaul, now a county of England. In Geoffrey's history its coast is where invaders land, Julius Caesar's legions first and later Hengist's Saxons.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Kingdom of Kent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_Kent)

## Kidaleta

Also: Kidaletam

A town on the north coast of Brittany where Cadwallon lands on his way to King Salomon in Geoffrey's story. It's taken for Aleth, the old walled town at Saint-Servan, beside Saint-Malo.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## Kimarcocus

Also: Kimarcocus

The earl of Tréguier in Geoffrey's story. In the great battle he charges with Hoel and Gawain toward the emperor's wedge, and falls there with two thousand of his men when the Romans surround them.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## Kimarcus

Also: Kinmarcus

Sisillius's son in Geoffrey's list of kings, who reigns after Jago and before Gorboduc, with nothing told of him but his name. Giles prints it *Kinmarcus*.

Wikipedia: [Kimarcus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kimarcus)

## Kimmare

Also: Kimmare dux Doroberniæ, Kimmare, duke of Canterbury

The duke of Canterbury in Geoffrey's story, one of the lords of the great cities who come to Arthur's crown-wearing in the City of the Legions. Among the heroes at the same court Geoffrey names another Kimmare.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## Kinarius

Also: Kimarus

Sisillius II's son and heir in Geoffrey's story, followed on the throne by his brother Danius. Nothing else is told of him, and Giles prints his name *Kimarus*.

Wikipedia: [Kinarius](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kinarius)

## Kincus

Also: Kincus

The bishop of Llanbadarn in Geoffrey's story, who becomes archbishop of the City of the Legions after Saint David dies. Geoffrey gives no more of him, and no other source names him.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## King David

Also: David rex

Israel's second king, who as a boy killed the giant Goliath and later took Jerusalem and made it his capital. The Psalms are credited to him, and Geoffrey dates Ebraucus's founding of York by his reign.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [David](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David)

## King Lot

Also: Lot de Londonesia, Lot of Lothian

Lot of Lothian, a brave knight of the Britons, wise and of mature years. King Uther gives him his daughter Anna, and the care of his kingdom while he's ill. Malory makes him Lot of Orkney, husband of Arthur's half-sister.

Wikipedia: [King Lot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Lot)

## King Louis of the Franks

Also: Ludovici

A king of the Franks in Geoffrey's story, the uncle who drives Isembard out of Gaul. Geoffrey names no particular Louis, and the Old French poem behind the story remembers Louis III, who beat the Vikings in 881 CE.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## Kymbelinus

Also: Kymbelinus

Tenvantius's son in Geoffrey's story, brought up at the court of Augustus, who pays Rome's tribute of his own free will and fathers Guiderius and Arvirargus. He's drawn from Cunobelinus, a real king of southeast Britain, and is Shakespeare's Cymbeline.

Wikipedia: [Cunobelinus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cunobelinus)

## Labienus

Also: Labienus

A Roman tribune in Geoffrey's story, killed by Nennius with Caesar's own sword. He comes from Quintus Laberius Durus, the tribune who fell fighting the Britons in Caesar's second invasion, whose name later histories turned into Labienus.

Wikipedia: [Quintus Laberius Durus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quintus_Laberius_Durus)

## Lam Goemagot

Also: Lamgoëmagot

Goemagot's Leap, the cliff from which Corineus throws the giant into the sea. Geoffrey says the place still gave birth to the name in his day; Giles's index puts it at the Hoe, in Plymouth.

Wikipedia: [Plymouth Hoe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plymouth_Hoe)

## Langres

Also: Lengrias

A hilltop town of northeastern France, in the Haute-Marne. In Geoffrey's story Lucius Tiberius shelters in it on his way to Autun, then marches out of it to meet Arthur in the valley of Suesia.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Langres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Langres)

## Latins

Also: Latinorum, Latinos

The people of Latium, around Rome in Italy, who spoke Latin. In Roman legend Aeneas came there from Troy and ruled them, and Geoffrey dates Brutus's city to the reign of their third king.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Latins (Italic tribe)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Latins_(Italic_tribe))

## Latinus

Also: a Latino rege, filiam Latini

The king of the Latins in Roman legend, who welcomed Aeneas when he came from Troy. His daughter Lavinia married Aeneas, and the kingdom of Italy passed to Aeneas with her, which is how Geoffrey traces Brutus's line.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Latinus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Latinus)

## Latinus Silvius

Also: Silvius Latinus, Silvium Latinum

A king of Alba Longa in Roman legend, the fourth in its line of kings. Geoffrey dates Ebraucus's founding of York by his reign, and names him again as the king before Alba Silvius.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Latinus Silvius](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Latinus_Silvius)

## Lavinia

Also: Laviniam, Laviniæ

Latinus's daughter, who in Roman legend married Aeneas after he came from Troy. In Geoffrey's story her marriage wins Aeneas the kingdom of Italy, and Brutus's mother is her niece.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Lavinia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lavinia)

## Le Mans

Also: Cenomanensis, Cenomannorum, Cenomanorum

A city of northwest France on the river Sarthe, the chief town of Maine, named after the Cenomani, the Gaulish people who lived there. In Geoffrey's story its lord, Borellus, comes to Arthur's court.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Le Mans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Le_Mans)

## Leicester

Also: Britannice Kaerleir, Leir-Cestre, Legecestriam, Kaerleir in British, Leircestre, urbe Kaerleir, Legecestria

The city on the river Soar in the English Midlands, Ratae Corieltauvorum to the Romans. Geoffrey says King Leir built it, and gives its British name as Kaerleir.

Wikipedia: [Leicester](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leicester)

## Leil

Also: Leil

Brutus Greenshield's son in Geoffrey's story, a king who loves peace and justice and builds Kaerleil, now Carlisle, in the north. He reigns twenty-five years but grows slack at the end, and civil war breaks out.

Wikipedia: [Leil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leil)

## Leir

Also: Leir filius, Leirum, Leir torpere, Leirem, Leiro, secum Leir

Bladud's son in Geoffrey's story, a king with three daughters and no son, who divides Britain between the two who flatter him and casts off Cordelia, who won't. Driven out by his sons-in-law, he goes to her in Gaul and wins back his kingdom with her husband's army. Shakespeare's King Lear is drawn from him.

Wikipedia: [Leir of Britain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leir_of_Britain)

## Leodegarius

Also: Leodegarius

The earl of Boulogne in Geoffrey's story, one of the lords from overseas at Arthur's crown-wearing in the City of the Legions. He isn't Saint Leodegar, the bishop of Autun of the seventh century.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## Leogecia

Also: Leogeciam

An uninhabited island, laid waste by pirates, where Brutus's fleet lands two days out from Greece and finds a ruined city with a temple of Diana. Wikipedia takes it for Lefkada, the Ionian island off western Greece, Leucadia in Latin, though Geoffrey's island is a legend's.

Wikipedia: [Lefkada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lefkada)

## Leolinus

Also: Leolinum, Leoninus

One of Helena's three uncles in Geoffrey's story, taken to Rome by Constantine and made a senator. Geoffrey later names him as the father of the senator Maximianus, which makes Maximianus a Briton on his father's side.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## Libra

Also: Pensa libræ

The scales, the seventh sign of the zodiac, which the sun enters in autumn, when day and night are the same length. In Merlin's prophecy its weights hang crooked until Aries the ram props them up.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Libra (astrology)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Libra_(astrology))

## Libya

Also: Libyæ

A country of North Africa, on the Mediterranean between Egypt and Tunisia; to Geoffrey's readers, Africa west of Egypt. Its king, Sertorius, marches with Lucius Tiberius in Geoffrey's story and dies by Arthur's hand.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Libya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Libya)

## Lincoln

Also: Lindocolinum, Lindocolinus, Kaerliudcoit

The cathedral city of Lincolnshire, in the east of England, Lindum to the Romans. In Geoffrey's story the Saxons take it, with London, York and Winchester, after the massacre at the peace meeting.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Lincoln, England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lincoln,_England)

## Lindsey

Also: Lindiseinensi, Londesia

The old kingdom of north Lincolnshire, between the Humber and the Witham. Geoffrey sets the city of Lincoln in it, besieged by the Saxons until Arthur comes to relieve it.

Wikipedia: [Kingdom of Lindsey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_Lindsey)

## Linligwan

Also: Linligwan

A pool near the Severn, in Wales, that Arthur tells Hoel about in Geoffrey's story. It swallows the sea's tide without filling, then spits it out in a wave as high as a mountain, and the History of the Britons calls it Oper Linn Liuan.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## Livius Gallus

Also: Livius Gallus, obsidebatque Gallum, suaserunt Gallo, præbens Gallus

Allectus's fellow commander in Geoffrey's story, who shuts the Romans left alive inside London and holds out against Asclepiodotus. Geoffrey says a London stream was named after him, the Walbrook.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [River Walbrook](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/River_Walbrook)

## Llanbadarn

Also: Lampaternensis

Llanbadarn Fawr, a village near Aberystwyth in west Wales, where Saint Padarn founded a monastery that was for a time a bishop's seat. In Geoffrey's story its bishop, Kincus, becomes archbishop after Saint David.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Llanbadarn Fawr](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Llanbadarn_Fawr)

## Llandaff

Also: Landaviæ

A district of Cardiff, in south Wales, around its cathedral, the seat of a bishop since the sixth century CE. In Geoffrey's story Chelianus, a priest of Llandaff, becomes archbishop of Dol.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Llandaff](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Llandaff)

## Loch Lomond

Also: stagnum Lumond, Lumond

The great loch of west central Scotland, north of Glasgow, with many islands. Geoffrey's Loch Lomond, from the History of the Britons' strange sights, has sixty islands, sixty rocks with eagles' nests and sixty rivers, and the Scots and Picts take refuge on its islands from Arthur.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Loch Lomond](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loch_Lomond)

## Locrinus

Also: Locrinus, Locrino, Locrinum, Locrine, Locrini

In Geoffrey's story, Brutus's firstborn son, who takes the middle of Britain and names it Loegria after himself. He drives out Humber the Hun and falls in love with the captive Estrildis, and he's killed in battle by the army of his wife, Gwendolen, after he leaves her.

Wikipedia: [Locrinus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Locrinus)

## Logres

Also: Loëgria, Loegriæ, Loegria

Geoffrey's name for the middle of Britain, roughly England, which he says Locrinus named after himself. It's his Latin for the Welsh name for England, and the French romances turn it into Logres.

Wikipedia: [Logres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Logres)

## Loire

Also: Ligeris

The longest river of France, flowing about 630 miles north and west through the middle of the country to the Atlantic. Brutus's fleet anchors in its mouth for seven days while his men explore the land.

Wikipedia: [Loire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loire)

## London

Also: Kaerlud, Londoniæ, Londoniis, Londonias, Londoniam, Londonia, Londoniarum, Londres, Kaerlondon, Londoniensis

The city on the Thames, the greatest town of Britain. Geoffrey says Brutus founded it as New Troy, and that King Lud rebuilt it and named it Kaerlud, the city of Lud, after himself, which became London.

Wikipedia: [London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London)

## Lothian

Also: Londonesiæ

The region of southeast Scotland around Edinburgh, between the Firth of Forth and the Tweed. Geoffrey's Lot rules it as an earl, and King Uther gives him his daughter Anna and the command of his army.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Lothian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lothian)

## Lucan

Also: Lucanus

A Roman poet of the first century CE, whose epic the *Pharsalia* tells the civil war between Julius Caesar and Pompey. Geoffrey quotes its line mocking Caesar for running from the Britons.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Lucan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lucan)

## Lucius

Also: nomen erat Lucius, rex Lucius, regis Lucii

Coillus's son in Geoffrey's story, the first Christian king of Britain, who asks Pope Eleutherius for baptism and has the pagan temples made into churches. He has no heir, and is buried in Gloucester.

Wikipedia: [Lucius of Britain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lucius_of_Britain)

## Lucius Catellus

Also: Lucius Catellus, Lucium Catellum

A Roman senator in Geoffrey's story who marches with Lucius Tiberius against Arthur. In the great battle he and Alifantinam, king of Spain, lead the first Roman wedge against Auguselus and Cador.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## Lucius Tiberius

Also: Lucii Tiberii, Lucius Reipublicæ, inquietationem Lucii, Lucius ergo Tiberius, Lucio Tiberio, ad Lucium, Lucius autem Tiberius, quam Lucius, At Lucius, Lucius Tiberius, aciem Lucii, cum Lucio, monitu Lucii, Lucius imperator, corpusque Lucii

The ruler of Rome in Geoffrey's story, procurator of the Republic, who writes to Arthur demanding the tribute Britain paid Julius Caesar and summoning him to Rome. He's Geoffrey's invention, and no Roman of that name ever ruled.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Lucius Tiberius](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lucius_Tiberius)

## Lud

Also: Lud

A later king of the Britons, Cassibellaunus's brother. He rebuilt Brutus's city with walls and towers and named it Kaerlud, the city of Lud, after himself, and the name became London, Geoffrey says.

Wikipedia: [King Lud](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Lud)

## Ludgate

Also: Parthlud, Ludesgata

The westernmost gate in London's walls, where the street up to St Paul's, Ludgate Hill, keeps its name. Geoffrey says King Lud was buried by it and that the Britons called it Parthlud, but its name probably comes from an Old English word for a back gate.

Wikipedia: [Ludgate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludgate)

## Lupus of Troyes

Also: Lupus Trecensis

Bishop of Troyes, in Gaul, who came to Britain with Germanus of Auxerre in 429 CE to argue down the followers of Pelagius. Geoffrey says the two restored the true faith among the Britons in Vortigern's time.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Lupus of Troyes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lupus_of_Troyes)

## Maddan

Also: Maddan

The son of Locrinus and Gwendolen in Geoffrey's story, raised by his grandfather Corineus. His mother hands him the kingdom once he's grown, and he rules Britain in peace for forty years, the father of Mempricius and Malin.

Wikipedia: [Maddan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maddan)

## Maelgwn Gwynedd

Also: Malgo, Malgone, Malgonis

Maelgwn, king of Gwynedd, in north Wales, in the 500s CE, one of the kings Gildas condemned. Geoffrey first names him as the king who has Saint David buried, and then makes him king of all Britain.

Wikipedia: [Maelgwn Gwynedd](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maelgwn_Gwynedd)

## Maglaurus

Also: Maglaunus, Maglauno

The duke of Albany in Geoffrey's story, Goneril's husband and Marganus's father. He and Henwinus take Leir's kingdom from him, and then he keeps Leir for two years with sixty knights. Giles prints his name *Maglaunus*.

Wikipedia: [Leir of Britain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leir_of_Britain)

## Maisbeli

Also: Maisbeli

The plain where Hengist plans to catch Aurelius's army by surprise in Geoffrey's story. Geoffrey doesn't say where it is; Wikipedia's Hengist and Horsa suggests Ballifield, near Sheffield in England.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Hengist and Horsa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hengist_and_Horsa)

## Maisuria

Also: Maisuriam

A field near Winchester, in Geoffrey's story, where Octavius meets the Roman army under Trahern. Geoffrey gives it as its British name, and no one has found which place he meant.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## Maleagant

Also: Maluasius

The king of Iceland in Geoffrey's story, Malvasius, who comes to Arthur's crown-wearing in the City of the Legions. Wikipedia's Maleagant takes him for the Meleagant of the French romances, but Geoffrey tells nothing of him beyond his name.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Maleagant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maleagant)

## Malin

Also: Malim

One of Maddan's two sons in Geoffrey's story. After their father dies, he and his brother Mempricius both want the throne, and Mempricius kills him at a meeting called to make peace.

Wikipedia: [Mempricius](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mempricius)

## Malva

Also: Malvæ

A river of North Africa, today's Moulouya in Morocco, which in Roman times marked the border between the two provinces of Mauretania. Geoffrey's Trojans cross it on their voyage west and land in Mauretania.

Wikipedia: [Moulouya River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moulouya_River)

## Malvern

Also: Malverniæ

The Malvern Hills, a ridge in Worcestershire, England, west of the Severn, rising high over the flat country around it. Merlin's prophecy names a serpent of Malvern that raises an ass.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Malvern Hills](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malvern_Hills)

## Marcellus Mutius

Also: Marcellus Mutius

A Roman in Geoffrey's story who chases Arthur's envoys to avenge Gaius Quintilianus. He catches up with Gawain, who turns and splits his helmet and head down to the chest.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## Marcia

Also: Marcia

Guithelin's queen in Geoffrey's story, a woman of high birth learned in every art, who writes the Marcian law and rules Britain for her young son Sisillius II after her husband dies. Geoffrey turns the Mercian law of the English into her work.

Wikipedia: [Queen Marcia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Queen_Marcia)

## Marcian law

Also: Martianam, Marcian law

The law Geoffrey says Queen Marcia drew up and King Alfred put into English as *Pa marchitie lage*. It's really the Mercian law, the custom of the Mercians of the English Midlands, which English lawyers of Geoffrey's day named beside the laws of Wessex and of the Danes.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Queen Marcia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Queen_Marcia)

## Margadud king of Dyfed

Also: Margadud rex Demetorum, Margadud rex Demetiorum

A king of Dyfed in Geoffrey's story, who helps drive Aethelfrith back from Bangor. Later, at Cadwallon's court, he advises Cadwallon to let Penda fight Oswiu, so the English will destroy one another.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## Margam

Also: videlicet Margan, Margan

A village near Port Talbot in South Wales, known for the abbey founded there in 1147 CE. Geoffrey says it takes its name from Marganus, killed there by his cousin Cunedagius.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Margam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Margam)

## Marganus

Also: Marganus videlicet, Marganum, Margano, Margani

Goneril and Maglaurus's son in Geoffrey's story, who with his cousin Cunedagius overthrows Cordelia and takes the north of Britain. Talked into taking the whole island, he's beaten by Cunedagius and killed in Wales, at the place Geoffrey says is named Margan after him.

Wikipedia: [Marganus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marganus)

## Marganus II

Also: Marganus Arthgallonis

Archgallo's son in Geoffrey's story, who keeps the Britons at peace, learning from his family's example. His brother Enniaunus succeeds him, and Wikipedia calls him Marganus II, since Leir's grandson has the same name.

Wikipedia: [Marganus II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marganus_II)

## Marius

Also: filius ejus Marius, petivit eum Marius, At Marius

Arvirargus's son in Geoffrey's story, a wise king who kills the Pictish king Rodric, gives his people Caithness to settle and pays Rome its tribute. He's known only from Geoffrey.

Wikipedia: [Marius of Britain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marius_of_Britain)

## Marius Lepidus

Also: Marius Lepidus, et Marium Lepidum

A Roman senator in Geoffrey's story who marches with Lucius Tiberius against Arthur. He helps lead a wedge with Hirtacius, king of the Parthians, and falls in the great battle.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## Marius the senator

Also: et Marium

One of Helena's three uncles in Geoffrey's story, taken to Rome by Constantine and made a senator. He shares his name with the earlier King Marius, Arvirargus's son, and Geoffrey tells nothing more of him.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## Mark the Evangelist

Also: Marcum Evangelistam

The writer the second gospel is named for. Church tradition makes him the founder of the church of Alexandria in Egypt. Geoffrey says the apostle Peter sent him there to preach.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Mark the Evangelist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mark_the_Evangelist)

## Mary

Also: Mariæ

Mary, the mother of Jesus, the most honored and prayed-to of all the saints in the Middle Ages. Arthur's shield Pridwen bears her painted image, to keep her always in his mind.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Mary, mother of Jesus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary,_mother_of_Jesus)

## Mauganius

Also: Mauganio

A bishop in Geoffrey's story, given the bishop's seat of Silchester when Arthur shares out the church's offices after his crown-wearing. Geoffrey tells nothing more of him here.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## Maugantius

Also: Maugantius, Maugantium

The learned man Vortigern asks whether a woman could conceive by no man. Maugantius answers from Apuleius that spirits living between the moon and the earth can take a man's shape and father children. He's known only from Geoffrey.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## Mauretania

Also: Mauritaniam

The Roman name for the northwest coast of Africa, in today's Morocco and western Algeria, after the Mauri, the Moors. Geoffrey's Trojans land there short of food and drink and plunder the country from end to end.

Wikipedia: [Mauretania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mauretania)

## Mauricius

Also: Mauricius, Mauricium, Mauricio

Caradocus's son in Geoffrey's story, a tall, bold man ready to prove his word in single combat, sent by his father to Rome to offer Maximianus the throne of Britain. He's known only from Geoffrey.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Eudaf Hen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eudaf_Hen)

## Mauricius Cadorcanensis

Also: Mauricium Cadorcanensem

One of four British nobles in Geoffrey's story killed in the Roman ambush on the escort taking the prisoners to Paris. He's another man than Caradocus's son Mauricius, who offers Maximianus the throne of Britain in Book V.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## Mauricius Silvanus

Also: Mauricium Silvanam

A Roman commander in Geoffrey's story, given a wedge of the third line in Lucius's army at the great battle. He's another man than Caradocus's son Mauricius, who offers Maximianus the throne of Britain in Book V.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## Mauron

Also: Mauron

The earl of Worcester in Geoffrey's story, one of the earls of the great cities who come to Arthur's crown-wearing in the City of the Legions. Geoffrey names him there alone.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## Maxentius

Also: Maxentius, Maxentio

The Roman emperor in Italy from 306 to 312 CE, beaten by Constantine at the Milvian Bridge outside Rome. In Geoffrey's story he's a tyrant who strips Rome's nobles of their property and drives them to Constantine in Britain.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Maxentius](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maxentius)

## Maximian

Also: Maximianus Herculius, Maximian Herculius

Diocletian's fellow emperor, who ruled the west from 286 to 305 CE and carried out his persecution of Christians there. Geoffrey calls him Herculius and the commander of Diocletian's army; he's another man than Maximianus.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Maximian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maximian)

## Maximianus

Also: Maximianus, Maximianum, Maximiano, Maximiani, Maximiane

A Roman senator in Geoffrey's story, the son of Helena's uncle Leolinus, invited to Britain to marry King Octavius's daughter and take the throne. Historians see him as Magnus Maximus, made emperor by his army in Britain in 383 CE.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Magnus Maximus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnus_Maximus)

## Medes

Also: Medorum, Medis

An ancient people of northwest Iran, conquered by the Persians in the 500s BCE. Geoffrey lists a king of the Medes among the eastern kings who come with Lucius against Arthur.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Medes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medes)

## Melga

Also: Melga, Melgæ

King of the Picts in Geoffrey's story, who with Wanius, king of the Huns, raids the coasts of Germany for Gratian and then invades Britain once its soldiers have gone. He's known only from Geoffrey.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Gracianus Municeps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gracianus_Municeps)

## Mempricius

Also: Mempricium et Malim, Mempricius autem, Mempricio

Maddan's son in Geoffrey's story, who murders his brother Malin at a peace meeting to take all of Britain. He rules as a tyrant, kills the nobles and leaves his wife, and after twenty years wolves kill him while he's out hunting.

Wikipedia: [Mempricius](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mempricius)

## Mempricius the Trojan

Also: Mempricius nomine

A leading Trojan in Greece who, when Brutus has King Pandrasus captive, stands up and advises the Trojans to ask for the king's daughter, ships and supplies and to leave Greece for good. He's known only from Geoffrey's story, and King Mempricius of Part 2 is another man.

## Mercia

Also: Merciorum
