The English kingdom of the Midlands, centered on the Trent. Geoffrey first names it as the kingdom of the pagan king Penda, in the wars of Cadwallon against the English.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Mercia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mercia)

## Mercury

Also: Mercurio, Mercurii, Mercurium

The Roman messenger god, god of travelers, trade and luck, Hermes to the Greeks. Brutus and his men honor him with Jupiter and Diana at the temple on Leogecia.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Mercury (mythology)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mercury_(mythology))

## Merianus

Also: Merianus

The king after Gurgintius in Geoffrey's list of the kings of Britain. Geoffrey tells nothing of him but his name and his place in the line, and Bledudo follows him.

Wikipedia: [Merianus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merianus)

## Merlin

Also: Merlinus, Merlinum, Merlino, Merlini, Ambrosio Merlino, Ambrosius Merlinus

A boy without a father, found at Carmarthen, whose mother is a king's daughter living as a nun. Vortigern's soothsayers say a fatherless boy's blood must be poured on the stones of his falling tower. Geoffrey calls him Merlin, also called Ambrosius.

Wikipedia: [Merlin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merlin)

## Micipsa

Also: Micipsa

The king of Babylon in Geoffrey's story, one of the rulers of the East who join Lucius Tiberius against Arthur. He falls in the great battle when the Britons charge after Bedivere's death.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## Minerva

Also: Minervæ

The Roman goddess of wisdom, crafts and the arts, the Greek Athena. Geoffrey hopes his book will be flavored with the salt of Robert of Gloucester's Minerva, meaning Robert's own learning.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Minerva](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minerva)

## Molmutine Laws

Also: Molmutinæ, Molmutinas

The laws Geoffrey says Dunvallo Molmutius gave the Britons, which made temples, cities, the roads to them and farmers' plows places of safety. Welsh law books of the Middle Ages also credit him, as Dyfnwal Moelmud, with laws older than Hywel the Good's.

Wikipedia: [Molmutine Laws](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Molmutine_Laws)

## Mont Saint-Michel

Also: Michaelis

A rocky tidal island off the coast of Normandy, crowned by an abbey of Saint Michael. In Geoffrey's story a giant from Spain carries Hoel's niece Helena to its top, and Arthur climbs it to kill him.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Mont-Saint-Michel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mont-Saint-Michel)

## Moray

Also: Mureif, Murefensium

A region of northeast Scotland, along the south shore of the Moray Firth. Geoffrey's Mureif is where the Scots and the Picts flee from Arthur, and the kingdom he gives to Urien, Lot's brother.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Moray](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moray)

## Mordred

Also: Modedrium, Modredo, Modredum, Modredus, Modredi

The son of Lot and Arthur's sister, Gawain's brother and Arthur's nephew, their son born in Aurelius Ambrosius's day. He's the Mordred of the later legend, the nephew who turns traitor in Arthur's last war.

Wikipedia: [Mordred](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mordred)

## Moriani

Also: Moranorum

A people in Geoffrey's story whose king lands in Northumbria and plunders it, until Morvidus beats him and kills every captive. Giles prints *Moranorum*, no people of that name is known, and Giles's index takes them for the Morini.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Morvidus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morvidus)

## Morini

Also: Morinorum

A people of the coast of Gaul facing Britain, around what's now Boulogne. Julius Caesar sailed from their country when he invaded Britain, and Geoffrey makes their duke Cheulfus a raider Brennius drives out.

Wikipedia: [Morini](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morini)

## Morvid

Also: Morvid

The earl of Gloucester in Geoffrey's story, first of the earls of the great cities who come to Arthur's crown-wearing in the City of the Legions. He isn't Morvidus, the cruel king of Part 3.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## Morvidus

Also: Morvidus

Danius's son by his mistress Tangustela in Geoffrey's story, a handsome, generous king and the strongest fighter in Britain, but so cruel he kills and skins his captives. He goes out alone against a sea monster from the Irish Sea, and it swallows him.

Wikipedia: [Morvidus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morvidus)

## Mount Aravius

Also: Aravium, Aravio monte

A mountain Merlin's prophecy names, where the lion of justice's eagle builds its nest. Geoffrey doesn't say where it is, and no one has placed it for certain.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## Mount Damen

Also: Damen

The steep hill where Uther's beaten army shelters for the night in Geoffrey's story, wooded with hazel on its top, with sheer rocks on its slopes. Geoffrey doesn't say where it is, and it hasn't been placed for certain.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## Mount Dolorous

Also: montem Dolosorum

A mountain where, in Geoffrey's story, King Ebraucus builds a town. Giles prints it *montem Dolosorum*, "the mountain of the deceitful," but it's known as Mount Dolorous, and nobody knows where it was.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## Mount Killaraus

Also: Killarao, Killaraum

The mountain in Ireland where the stones of the Giants' Dance stand in Geoffrey's story, until Merlin and Uther come for them. Giles's index takes it for Kildare, but nobody has placed it for certain.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Mount Killaraus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Killaraus)

## Nathan

Also: Nathan

The prophet at King David's court who called David out for taking Bathsheba and having her husband killed, and who later backed Solomon as heir. Geoffrey names him with Gad and Asaph.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Nathan (prophet)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nathan_(prophet))

## Nennius

Also: Nennium, Nennio, Nennius

Lud's brother, angry that Lud wished to wipe out the name of Troy by renaming New Troy after himself. Geoffrey says Gildas told their quarrel at length, which no surviving book of Gildas does.

Wikipedia: [Nennius of Britain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nennius_of_Britain)

## Nero

Also: Neroni

The Roman emperor from 54 to 68 CE. Geoffrey names him where Juvenal's satire speaks of the emperor Domitian, mocked there as a bald Nero.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Nero](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nero)

## Normandy

Also: Neustriensium, Neustria, Neustriam, Neustriæ, Normannia, Normanniæ, Neustriensibus

The region of northern France on the Channel coast. Geoffrey calls it Neustria, the name of the western Frankish kingdom before the Norsemen settled there in the 900s CE, and Brennius fits out his fleet on its coast.

Wikipedia: [Normandy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Normandy)

## Northumbria

Also: Northumbriam, Northumbriæ, Northanhumbriæ, Northanhumbriam, Northamhumbriæ, Northanhumbrorum

The English kingdom north of the Humber, stretching in its greatest days from the Humber to the Firth of Forth. Geoffrey uses the name even for that land in the far-off reigns before the English came.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Northumbria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northumbria)

## Norway

Also: Norwegiam, Norwegiæ, Norwegense

The kingdom on the western side of Scandinavia. In Geoffrey's story Brennius sails there to marry its king's daughter and comes back with a Norwegian army to fight his brother Belinus.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Norway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norway)

## Norwegians

Also: Norwegensium, Norwegenses, Norwegensibus

The people of Norway. Geoffrey has Brennius raise a Norwegian army to win back his share of Britain, and Belinus beats it in the forest of Calaterium, where fifteen thousand men die.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Norwegians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norwegians)

## Octa

Also: Octa, Octam, Octæ

Hengist's son, who Hengist invites over from Germany with Ebissa, asking Vortigern to give them lands in the north of Britain. The kings of Kent later traced their line from him.

Wikipedia: [Octa of Kent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Octa_of_Kent)

## Octavius

Also: Octavius, Octavium, Octavio

Duke of the Gewisse in Geoffrey's story, who kills Rome's governors and makes himself king of Britain, loses his crown to Trahern and wins it back. Welsh tradition knows him as Eudaf Hen, Eudaf the Old.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Eudaf Hen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eudaf_Hen)

## Odnea

Also: Odnea

The place on the coast of Gaul where Geoffrey says Julius Caesar built a tower as a refuge, in case the Gauls rose against him again. No such place is known.

Wikipedia: [Tower of London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tower_of_London)

## Oenus

Also: Oenus

The king after Cap in Geoffrey's list of the kings of Britain. Geoffrey tells nothing of him but his name and his place in the line, and Sisillius III follows him.

Wikipedia: [Oenus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oenus)

## Oethelwald

Also: Ethelwaldus, Ethelwaldum

Oswald's son, a king of Deira who sided with Penda against his uncle Oswiu, and stood aside from the battle at the Winwaed in 655 CE. In Geoffrey's story he and Alhfrith rise against Oswiu and flee to Penda.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Œthelwald of Deira](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C5%92thelwald_of_Deira)

## Olbrictus

Also: Olbrictus

The king of Norway in Geoffrey's story, on Arthur's side in the last battle against Mordred. He falls there with Aschillius, king of Denmark, and many thousands of their men. He's known from this one passage.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## Old English

Also: Saxonica, Saxonice

The language of the English before the Norman Conquest, which Geoffrey names after the Saxons. He gives English names beside British ones, as *Ludesgata* for the gate the Britons called Parthlud, and *Pa marchitie lage* for Marcia's law.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Old English](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_English)

## Orion

Also: Orion

A giant hunter of Greek myth set among the stars, and the bright winter constellation named for him, with the three stars of his belt and the sword that hangs from it. Merlin's prophecy has iron Orion bare that sword.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Orion (constellation)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orion_(constellation))

## Orkney

Also: Orcades, Orcadum

The islands off the north tip of mainland Scotland. Geoffrey's history names them among the lands the early British kings rule over, and later makes their king one of Arthur's vassals.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Orkney](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orkney)

## Osfrith

Also: Offridus

Edwin's son, killed with his father in battle against Cadwallon and Penda in 633 CE. Geoffrey tells the same deaths, and sets the battle at Heavenfield, where Bede has Hatfield Chase.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## Osric

Also: Osrico

A king of Deira, in southern Northumbria, who succeeded Edwin in 633 CE and was killed by Cadwallon the next year. Geoffrey tells the same death, and adds two nephews who should have ruled after him.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Osric of Deira](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Osric_of_Deira)

## Oswald

Also: Oswaldus, Oswaldo, Oswaldum

King of the Northumbrians from 634 CE, a Christian who the English honored as a saint. In Geoffrey's story he takes Northumbria's throne after Edwin and is hunted by Cadwallon.

Wikipedia: [Oswald of Northumbria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oswald_of_Northumbria)

## Oswiu

Also: Oswius, Oswio, Oswium

Oswald's brother, who becomes king of the Northumbrians after him in 642 CE. Geoffrey says he made his peace with Cadwallon, then lord of all Britain, with gifts of gold and silver.

Wikipedia: [Oswiu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oswiu)

## Owain son of Urien

Also: Eventus filius

Urien's son, a king of the northern Britons in the late 500s CE, praised by the poet Taliesin. Geoffrey makes him Auguselus's nephew, who takes the kingdom of Albany when Auguselus falls fighting Mordred. The romances and Malory remember him as Ywain, a knight of the Round Table.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Owain mab Urien](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Owain_mab_Urien)

## Panchaia

Also: Panchaii

An island Greek and Roman writers placed in the sea east of Arabia, rich in incense and precious stones, whose place has never been found. Merlin's prophecy has its mountains shake.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Panchaia (island)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Panchaia_(island))

## Pandrasus

Also: Pandrasi, Pandrasus, Pandraso

The king of the Greeks in Geoffrey's story, who holds the descendants of the Trojans captured at Troy as slaves. He's known only from this legend of Brutus.

Wikipedia: [Pandrasus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pandrasus)

## Pandrasus king of Egypt

Also: Pandrasus rex Ægypti, Pandrasum regem Ægypti

The king of Egypt in Geoffrey's story, an ally of Lucius Tiberius, and another man than the Greek king Pandrasus that Brutus defeats in Book I. In the great battle he commands a wedge of the Romans' second line.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## Paris

Also: Parisios

The capital of France, on the river Seine, which the Romans called Lutetia, the city of the Parisii. In Geoffrey's story Frollo takes refuge there from Arthur, and Arthur later holds court there once all Gaul is his.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Paris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paris)

## Parthians

Also: Parthorum

The people of Parthia, in northeastern Iran, whose empire was Rome's great rival in the east for nearly three hundred years. Geoffrey lists their king among the eastern kings who come with Lucius against Arthur, though Parthia had fallen centuries before.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Parthia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parthia)

## Partholón

Also: Partholoim

The leader of a people driven out of Spain in Geoffrey's story, who meets Gurguit Barbtruc at sea off Orkney with thirty ships and asks for somewhere to settle. Gurguit gives them Ireland, empty then, and Geoffrey says they've held it ever since. Irish legend makes Partholón the first settler of Ireland after the Flood.

Wikipedia: [Partholón](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parthol%C3%B3n)

## Pasgen

Also: Pascentius, Pascentio, Pascentium

Vortigern's third son, named with his brothers Vortimer and Catigern, who Geoffrey calls Pascentius. Welsh tradition remembered him as a lord of Builth and Gwrtheyrnion, in mid Wales.

Wikipedia: [Pasgen ap Cadeyrn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pasgen_ap_Cadeyrn)

## Patrick

Also: Patricius

A Briton carried off as a boy to slavery in Ireland, who escaped, became a priest and went back to turn the Irish to Christ in the 400s CE. Geoffrey says he founded the abbey where Saint David died, and had predicted David's birth.

Wikipedia: [Saint Patrick](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint_Patrick)

## Pelagianism

Also: Pelagianam hæresim, Pelagian heresy

The teaching of Pelagius, a British monk in Rome around 400 CE, that people can choose to do good by their own will. The Church condemned it as a heresy in 418, and Geoffrey says it had spoiled the Britons' faith until Germanus and Lupus came to preach.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## Pellitus

Also: Pellitus, Pelliti

A seer from Spain in Geoffrey's story, who reads the flight of birds and the stars and warns King Edwin of every attack before it comes. Brian kills him at York with an iron staff, disguised as a beggar.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Pellitus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pellitus)

## Penda

Also: Peanda, Peandam, Peandæ

The pagan king of the Mercians, in the English Midlands, the most warlike English king of the 600s CE. Geoffrey's Penda lays siege to Exeter, where Cadwallon's nephew Brian holds out.

Wikipedia: [Penda of Mercia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Penda_of_Mercia)

## Peredurus

Also: Peredurus, Pereduro, Pereduri

Morvidus's youngest son in Geoffrey's story, who with Ingenius imprisons their brother Elidurus and then holds all Britain when Ingenius dies. He rules so kindly that people forget Elidurus, until he dies suddenly.

Wikipedia: [Peredurus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peredurus)

## Periron

Also: Perironis

A river Merlin's prophecy names, which an old man white as snow turns aside to build a mill over. Geoffrey doesn't say where it is, and no one has placed it for certain.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## Petreius

Also: Petreio, Petreium, Petreius

A Roman senator in Geoffrey's story, Petreius Cotta. He comes to rescue the Romans chasing Arthur's envoys and leads them like a good general, until Boso of Oxford throws his arms around his neck, pulls him to the ground and takes him prisoner.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## Philistines

Also: Philisteis

A people of the coast of Canaan, in today's Gaza and southern Israel, the Israelites' great enemies in the Bible's books of Judges and Samuel. Geoffrey dates Brutus's city to the time they captured the Ark of the Covenant in battle.

Wikipedia: [Philistines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philistines)

## Phoebus

Also: Phœbus

Phoebus, "the bright one," is a name of Apollo, the Greek and Roman god of the sun, light and prophecy. Merlin's prophecy names a Phoebus of the sea among the planets and stars, and doesn't say why.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Apollo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apollo)

## Phrygia

Also: Phrygiæ, Phyrgiæ

An ancient kingdom of west central Asia Minor, in what's now Turkey. In Geoffrey's story its duke, Teucer, marches with Lucius Tiberius against Arthur and commands a wedge in the great battle.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Phrygia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phrygia)

## Picts

Also: Pictis, Picti, Pictorum, Pictos

The people of eastern and northern Scotland beyond the Roman walls, whose name in Latin means "painted people." Geoffrey counts them among the island's five peoples, and says the Britons, for their pride, gave way before them and the Saxons.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Picts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Picts)

## Pillars of Hercules

Also: columnas Herculis

The two headlands on either side of the Strait of Gibraltar, the Rock of Gibraltar and a mountain in Morocco opposite, which Greek myth said Hercules set up at the end of the known world. Geoffrey's Trojans sail to them and are nearly sunk there by the Sirens.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Pillars of Hercules](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pillars_of_Hercules)

## Pinner

Also: Ymnerem

A king of Loegria in Geoffrey's story, in the years of civil war, killed in battle by Dunvallo Molmutius. Giles prints his name *Ymner*, and Wikipedia calls him Pinner.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Staterius](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Staterius)

## Pir

Also: cui Pir

The king after Samuil Penissel in Geoffrey's list of the kings of Britain. Geoffrey tells nothing of him but his name and his place in the line, and Capoir follows him.

Wikipedia: [Pir of the Britons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pir_of_the_Britons)

## Pleiades

Also: Pleiades

A cluster of stars in the constellation Taurus, also called the Seven Sisters, named for seven sisters of Greek myth that Zeus set in the sky. Merlin's prophecy has them burst into tears.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Pleiades](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pleiades)

## Poitevins

Also: Pictavensium, Pictavensibus, Pictavensis, Poitou

The people of Poitou, around Poitiers in west central France, named after the Pictones, the Gaulish people who lived there in Roman times. Geoffrey makes Goffarius, king of Aquitaine, their lord.

Wikipedia: [Poitou](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poitou)

## Polytetes

Also: Polytetes, Polytetem

The duke of Bithynia in Geoffrey's story, an ally of Lucius Tiberius. He commands a wedge of the Romans' second line in the great battle, where Arthur cuts off his head with Excalibur.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## Pompey

Also: Pompeium

Pompey the Great, a Roman general who was Julius Caesar's ally and then his rival. Caesar beat him in the civil war, and he was killed in Egypt in 48 BCE. Geoffrey has Caesar march against him after Britain.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Pompey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pompey)

## Pope Eleutherius

Also: Eleutherio Papæ, Eleutherii papæ

The bishop of Rome from about 174 to 189 CE. Bede and Geoffrey say King Lucius wrote asking him for baptism, and that he sent teachers to Britain, Fagan and Deruvian in Geoffrey's telling.

Wikipedia: [Pope Eleutherius](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pope_Eleutherius)

## Pope Sergius

Also: Sergium, Sergio

Sergius I, pope from 687 to 701 CE, who baptized Caedwalla, king of the West Saxons, in Rome. In Geoffrey's story an angel sends Cadwaladr to him, and he confirms Cadwaladr before Cadwaladr dies in Rome.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Pope Sergius I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pope_Sergius_I)

## Pope Sulpicius

Also: Sulpicii Papæ

A pope who, Geoffrey says, took the boy Gawain into his household at Arthur's wish and gave him his arms. No pope of that name ever sat in Rome; the Latin romance of Gawain's boyhood, De Ortu Waluuanii, tells the same.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [De Ortu Waluuanii](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/De_Ortu_Waluuanii)

## Porrex

Also: Porrex

Gorboduc's son in Geoffrey's story, who plots to kill his brother Ferrex and then kills him in battle. Their mother, Judon, who loved Ferrex more, attacks Porrex in his sleep with her maids and hacks him to pieces.

Wikipedia: [Porrex I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Porrex_I)

## Porrex II

Also: Post Porrecem

The king after Coillus in Geoffrey's list, followed by Cherin. Geoffrey tells nothing of him but his name, and Wikipedia calls him Porrex II, since Gorboduc's son has the same name.

Wikipedia: [Porrex II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Porrex_II)

## Porsenna

Also: Porsena, Porsenæ

The other of the two consuls governing Rome in Geoffrey's story, captured when Belinus and Brennius take Rome. Geoffrey borrows the name of Lars Porsena, the Etruscan king Roman legend says besieged Rome, and Giles prints it *Porsena*.

Wikipedia: [Belinus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Belinus)

## Portchester

Also: Porcestriam, Kaerperis, Portcestria

A village on Portsmouth Harbour in Hampshire, around a Roman fort whose walls still stand. Geoffrey has Claudius land and lay siege there, and gives its British name as Kaerperis.

Wikipedia: [Portchester](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portchester)

## Portunienses

Also: Portuniensium

A people of Gaul in Geoffrey's story who send men to Arthur's war on Rome, named with the Ruteni, the Estrusienses and the men of Le Mans, Anjou and Poitou. Nobody has placed them for sure.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## Priam

Also: Priami

The last king of Troy in Greek legend, the father of Hector, Paris and many other sons, killed when the Greeks took Troy. Geoffrey traces the enslaved Trojans in Greece to his son Helenus, and Brutus to his line.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Priam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Priam)

## Pridwen

Also: Priwen

Arthur's shield in Geoffrey's story, painted with an image of Mary, which he carries into the battle at Bath. In the Welsh tales the name Prydwen belongs to Arthur's ship, and Geoffrey gives it to his shield.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Pridwen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pridwen)

## Pyramus

Also: Pyramum

Arthur's chaplain in Geoffrey's story, the priest of his household. When Arthur finds York's churches burned and its archbishop driven out by the Saxons, he makes Pyramus archbishop of York in his place.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## Pyrrhus

Also: Pyrrhus

Achilles's son, called Pyrrhus as well as Neoptolemus, one of the Greeks who sacked Troy. Geoffrey says he carried Helenus and many other Trojans off to Greece in chains, to avenge his father's death.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Neoptolemus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neoptolemus)

## Queen of Sheba

Also: regina Saba

A queen in the Bible who tested Solomon's wisdom with hard questions. She brought him gold and spices from her far country. Geoffrey dates the reign of King Leil by her visit.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## Quintus Carutius

Also: Quintus Carutius, Quintum Carutium, Quintum Carucium

A Roman senator in Geoffrey's story who marches with Lucius Tiberius against Arthur. He helps lead the ambush on the Britons taking the prisoners to Paris, and commands a wedge of the Romans' third line.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## Quintus Milvius Catulus

Also: Quintus Milvius Catulus, quintum Milvium, Quintus quoque Milvius

A Roman senator in Geoffrey's story who marches with Lucius Tiberius against Arthur. He helps lead a wedge of the front line with Sertorius, king of Libya, and falls in the great battle.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## Redechius

Also: Rederchius

The king after Redon in Geoffrey's list of the kings of Britain. Geoffrey tells nothing of him but his name and his place in the line, and Giles prints it *Rederchius*.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Redechius](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Redechius)

## Redon

Also: Redion

The king after Eldol in Geoffrey's list of the kings of Britain. Geoffrey tells nothing of him but his name and his place in the line, and Giles prints it *Redion*.

Wikipedia: [Redon of Britain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Redon_of_Britain)

## Regan

Also: Regau

Leir's second daughter in Geoffrey's story, who swears she loves him above every living thing and is married to Henwinus of Cornwall. When Leir comes to stay with her, she cuts his knights to five.

Wikipedia: [Regan (King Lear)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Regan_(King_Lear))

## Remus

Also: Remo

Romulus's twin brother in Roman legend, raised with him by a she-wolf. Romulus killed him as the city was being founded. Geoffrey names both twins as the founders of Rome.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Romulus and Remus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Romulus_and_Remus)

## Rennes

Also: Redonum

The chief city of Brittany, in northwest France, on the Vilaine river. In Geoffrey's story it's the first city Maximianus and Conan take in Armorica.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Rennes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rennes)

## Rhitta

Also: Rithonem

A giant of the Welsh tales, Geoffrey's Ritho, who made a cloak of the beards of kings he'd beaten. He asks Arthur for his beard, and Arthur kills him in single combat, on Mount Aravius in Geoffrey's telling.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Giants (Welsh folklore)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Giants_(Welsh_folklore))

## Ricaradoch

Also: Ricaradoch

The place Geoffrey names Uther's friend Ulfin after, calling him Ulfin of Ricaradoch when Uther tells him of his love for Igraine. Geoffrey says nothing more of it, and it hasn't been placed for certain.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## Richborough

Also: Rutupi portum

A port in Kent, the Romans' Rutupiae, where Claudius's army landed in 43 CE and the Romans kept their chief harbor for Gaul. Geoffrey has Julius Caesar land there, and Vespasian try to.

Wikipedia: [Richborough](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richborough)

## Richerius

Also: Richerium

One of Arthur's earls in Geoffrey's story. With Cador, Bedivere and Borellus he escorts the Roman prisoners toward Paris, and when the Romans ambush them he and Bedivere guard the captives.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## Richiden

Also: Richiden

Geoffrey's British name for Oxford, which he says the Saxons call Oxineford. Its earl, Boso, commands a division with Guerinus of Chartres in Arthur's army at the great battle with Lucius Tiberius.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## Riculf

Also: Riculfum, Riculfus

The man the Norwegians make their king in Geoffrey's story, refusing Lot, the heir Sichelm named. He fortifies Norway's cities and meets Arthur on the shore with the whole people of the land.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [King Lot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Lot)

## Ridoc

Also: Ridocensis

Geoffrey's British name for Oxford, the university city on the Thames, in southern England, given beside its English name in the list of earls at Arthur's court. The Welsh Brut Tysilio calls it Rydychen.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Oxford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oxford)

## Rivallo

Also: Rivallo

Cunedagius's son and heir in Geoffrey's story, a peaceful, lucky young king who governs with care. In his time it rains blood for three days, and swarms of flies kill people.

Wikipedia: [Rivallo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rivallo)

## River Barba

Also: Barbæ fluvii

The river in Gaul with the port where, Geoffrey says, Arthur orders his kings to gather their armies by the first of August for the march on Rome. Geoffrey doesn't say where it is, and it hasn't been placed for sure.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## River Darent

Also: Derwent

A river in Kent that flows north into the Thames near Dartford. Geoffrey's Vortimer fights the first of his battles against the Saxons on it, and the History of the Britons calls it the Derguentid.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## River Douglas

Also: Duglas

A river of Lancashire and Greater Manchester, in northwest England, that runs into the Ribble estuary. In Geoffrey's story Arthur fights his first battle against Colgrin's Saxons, Scots and Picts beside it, the Dubglas of the History of the Britons.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## River Stour

Also: Sturam, by the Stour

A river where, in Geoffrey's story, Gwendolen's army meets Locrinus's and he's killed by an arrow. England has several rivers called Stour, and Geoffrey doesn't say which he means.

## Robert of Gloucester

Also: Roberte dux Claudiocestriæ

Robert, Earl of Gloucester, the oldest of King Henry I's children born outside marriage and one of the great lords of England in the 1100s CE. Geoffrey dedicates his book to him, praising his learning and his skill in war.

Wikipedia: [Robert, 1st Earl of Gloucester](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert,_1st_Earl_of_Gloucester)

## Rodric

Also: Rodric

A king of the Picts in Geoffrey's story who sails from Scythia, lands in Albany and lays it waste until Marius kills him. His people are given Caithness to settle.

Wikipedia: [Marius of Britain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marius_of_Britain)

## Romans

Also: Romanis, Romani, Romanorum, Romanos

The people of Rome and its empire, who conquered most of Britain in the first century CE and ruled it for nearly four hundred years. Geoffrey still counts them among Britain's five peoples, and his history brings Britons and Romans to war more than once.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Ancient Rome](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ancient_Rome)

## Rome

Also: Romam, Romæ, Roma, Romulea domus, Romamque

The city in central Italy that ruled an empire stretching from Britain to Syria. Geoffrey sets its founding by Romulus and Remus in the reign of an early British king, and makes it Britain's great rival for centuries after.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Rome](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rome)

## Romulus

Also: Romulo

The legendary founder and first king of Rome, said to have been raised with his twin brother Remus by a she-wolf. Geoffrey dates the reign of Cunedagius by their founding of Rome.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Romulus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Romulus)

## Ron

Also: Ron

Arthur's spear in Geoffrey's story, long and broad and made for slaughter, which he carries into the battle at Bath. The name is short for Rhongomyniad, Arthur's spear in the Welsh tales, from the Welsh word for a spear.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Rhongomyniad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhongomyniad)

## Rowena

Also: Rowena, Rowenam, Rowenæ

Hengist's daughter, who comes over from Germany with his new soldiers. At her father's feast she brings Vortigern a cup of wine and greets him in English, and he falls in love with her and gives Hengist Kent for her. Later she has her stepson Vortimer poisoned.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Rowena](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rowena)

## Rudaucus

Also: Rudaucus

A king of Wales in Geoffrey's story, in the years of civil war, who allies with Staterius of Albany against Dunvallo Molmutius. He's killed when Dunvallo's men, wearing the enemy's armor, reach him.

Wikipedia: [Dyfnwal Moelmud](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dyfnwal_Moelmud)

## Runo

Also: Runno

Peredurus's son in Geoffrey's story, who succeeds his cousin Idvallo as king of Britain. Geoffrey tells nothing of him but his name and his place in the line, and Giles prints him *Runno*.

Wikipedia: [King Runo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Runo)

## Rusicada

Also: Ruscicadam

A Roman port on the coast of North Africa, today's Skikda, in northeastern Algeria. Geoffrey's Trojans sail between it and the mountains of Azara, where pirates attack them and are beaten.

Wikipedia: [Skikda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skikda)

## Ruteni

Also: Rutenorum, Rutenos

A Gallic people of southern Gaul, living around what's now Rodez, conquered by the Romans. Geoffrey puts Julius Caesar on their coast when he first looks across at Britain, though their lands lay far from the sea.

Wikipedia: [Ruteni](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ruteni)

## Rutuli

Also: Rutulorum

An ancient people of Latium, in Italy, south of Rome, centered on Ardea. In Roman legend and in Virgil's *Aeneid* their king Turnus fought Aeneas for the hand of Lavinia, and lost.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Rutuli](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rutuli)

## Sabines

Also: Sabinæ, Sabine

An ancient people of the hills northeast of Rome, whose daughters, Roman legend says, Romulus's men carried off for wives. Geoffrey says Ebraucus's daughters married the Trojans that the Sabine and Latin women refused.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Sabines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sabines)

## Sagittarius

Also: Sagittarii

The archer, the ninth sign of the zodiac, drawn as a centaur, half man and half horse, drawing a bow. In Merlin's prophecy Virgo climbs on the archer's back.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Sagittarius (astrology)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sagittarius_(astrology))

## Saint Eldad

Also: beatus Eldadus, Aderat Eldadus, Eldadus Episcopus, Eldadi sententiæ, Eldadi Episcopi

A holy man of the Britons in Geoffrey's story, bishop of Gloucester and brother of Eldol, its earl. He buries the lords murdered at Hengist's peace meeting in the Christian way, in the cemetery by Ambrius's monastery near Salisbury, and later gives Aurelius his judgment on the beaten Saxons. He isn't Part 3's King Edadus, nor the Eldad of Ebraucus's sons.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Eldol, Consul of Gloucester](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eldol,_Consul_of_Gloucester)

## Saint Martin

Also: sancti Martini

Martin, bishop of Tours in the 300s CE, a soldier turned monk and one of the best-loved saints of the Middle Ages. Geoffrey says the Britons built a church in his honor beneath the bronze figure that held King Cadwallon's body over London's west gate.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Martin of Tours](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_of_Tours)

## Saint Peter

Also: Petrus, Petri, Petrus Apostolus, sancti Petri

Peter the apostle, the leader of Jesus's twelve followers, who tradition makes the first bishop of Rome. Geoffrey dates his founding of the church at Antioch and his coming to Rome to the reign of the British king Arviragus.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Saint Peter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint_Peter)

## Salinae

Also: locum Salinarum

A place on the North African coast that Geoffrey's Trojans pass, its name meaning "the salt pans." Giles's index takes it for salt works in Tripoli, but no identification is secure.

## Salisbury

Also: Salesberia, Kaercaradane, Kaercaradoc, Saleberiensis, Salesberiensis

The town in Wiltshire, in southern England, near the old hill fort of Old Sarum and the stones of Stonehenge. Geoffrey says the British lords Hengist's men murdered were buried near it, at the monastery of Abbot Ambrius, at a place then called Kaercaradoc.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Salisbury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salisbury)

## Salomon king of Brittany

Also: Salomonem, Salomon, Salomonis

The king of the Britons of Brittany in Geoffrey's story, who raises Cadwallon and Edwin at his court. Later he takes in the exiled Cadwallon, asks why the Britons have lost their island, and gives him ten thousand soldiers to win it back.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## Samson of Dol

Also: sancti Samsonis, Saint Samson

A Welsh monk of the sixth century CE who crossed to Brittany and founded the monastery of Dol, one of the founding saints of Brittany. Geoffrey makes him archbishop of Dol, the seat Chelianus takes after him.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## Samson of York

Also: Samsoni illustri viro, Samson, beato Samsone

A famous holy man, known for his devotion, who Aurelius makes archbishop of York in Geoffrey's story when the seat stands empty after the Saxon wars. He isn't Samson the judge of Israel, nor Saint Samson of Dol.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## Samuel

Also: Samuel, Samuelem

The last of the judges who led Israel before it had kings, a prophet who anointed Saul as its first king and later David in Saul's place. Geoffrey dates Gwendolen's reign by him.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Samuel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel)

## Samuil Penissel

Also: Samuilpenissel

The king after Redechius in Geoffrey's list of the kings of Britain. Wikipedia's article on Sawyl Penuchel, "high-head," a king of the Britons after the Romans left, gives Samuil Penissel, "low-head," as another of his names.

Wikipedia: [Sawyl Penuchel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sawyl_Penuchel)

## Satan

Also: Satana, Satanas, Satanæ

The devil by name, the fallen angel Christians hold rules over hell and tempts people to sin. Geoffrey says Satan entered Vortigern's heart when, drunk at Hengist's feast, he fell in love with Hengist's pagan daughter.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Satan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Satan)

## Sater

Also: Sater

The ruler of Dyfed and the South Welsh in Geoffrey's story. He comes to Arthur's crown-wearing in the City of the Legions with the other kings of Britain, but Geoffrey tells nothing more of him.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## Saturn

Also: Saturnum, Saturni

The Roman god of the harvest and of a golden age, the father of Jupiter in Roman myth. Hengist names him first among the gods his people worship when Vortigern asks the Saxons their religion.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Saturn (mythology)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturn_(mythology))

## Saul

Also: Saul

Israel's first king, anointed by the prophet Samuel, who fought the Philistines all his reign and lost the throne to David. Geoffrey dates the death of Mempricius by his reign.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Saul](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saul)

## Saxons

Also: Saxonibus, Saxones, Saxonum, Saxonibusque

The Germanic people from the North Sea coast who settled Britain in the 400s and 500s CE and became the English. Geoffrey counts them among the island's five peoples, and says the Britons lost the land to them and the Picts for their pride, a fall his history tells at length.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Saxons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saxons)

## Scaeva

Also: Scævam

Androgeus's son in Geoffrey's story. His father sends him to Julius Caesar as a hostage, with thirty young men of his family, so that Caesar will trust him and cross to Britain again.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Mandubracius](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mandubracius)

## Scorpio

Also: Scorpionis

The scorpion, the eighth sign of the zodiac, which the sun enters in late autumn, named for the constellation Scorpius. In Merlin's prophecy the scorpion's tail breeds lightning.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Scorpio (astrology)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scorpio_(astrology))

## Scotland

Also: Scotia, Scotiam, Scotiæ, Scotiamque

The land in the north of Britain, beyond the old Roman walls. Geoffrey says that in his own day the country Albanactus called Albany after himself was called Scotland.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Scotland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scotland)

## Scots

Also: Scotis, Scoti, Scotorum, Scotos

The Gaelic-speaking people the Romans called *Scoti*, who came from Ireland and settled the west of what's now Scotland, which took its name from them. Geoffrey names them last of the island's five peoples, beside the Romans, Britons, Saxons and Picts.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Scoti](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scoti)

## Scythia

Also: Scythia, Scythiam

The ancients' name for the wide lands north of the Black Sea, home of horse-riding nomads. Geoffrey says the Picts came from it, sailing to Britain under their king Rodric.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Scythia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scythia)

## Seginus

Also: Seginum

The duke of the Allobroges in Geoffrey's story, who takes in Brennius when no other prince of Gaul will help him. He marries Brennius to his only daughter, Brennius becomes duke when he dies, and Seginus is known only from Geoffrey.

Wikipedia: [Brennius](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brennius)

## Senones

Also: Senonesque, Senonian Gauls

A Gallic people, and about 390 BCE an army of Gauls led by Brennus, one of their chiefs, beat the Romans at the river Allia and took Rome. In Geoffrey's story the Romans take Belinus's army for Brennius's Senonian Gauls.

Wikipedia: [Senones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Senones)

## Serses

Also: Serses, Sersem

The king of Iturea in Geoffrey's story, one of the rulers of the East who join Lucius Tiberius against Arthur. In the great battle he commands one of the four wedges of the Romans' second line.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## Sertorius

Also: Sertorius, Sertorium

The king of Libya in Geoffrey's story, an ally of Lucius Tiberius. He helps lead the ambush on the Britons taking the prisoners to Paris, and in the great battle Arthur cuts off his head with Excalibur.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## Severn

Also: Sabrinæ, Sabrinum, Sabrinam, Sabrina, Sabrino

The longest river of Britain, about 220 miles, flowing from the hills of mid Wales out into the Bristol Channel. Geoffrey names it with the Thames and the Humber as the island's three great rivers, along which ships bring trade from every nation.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [River Severn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/River_Severn)

## Severus

Also: Severus, Severum

Septimius Severus, the Roman emperor who came to Britain in 208 CE and died at York in 211 CE. In Geoffrey he's a senator Rome sends with two legions to win the island back, who fights the Britons under Fulgenius.

Wikipedia: [Septimius Severus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Septimius_Severus)

## Shaftesbury

Also: montis Paladur, Sefovia, Mount Paladur, Sehstoniæ

A hilltop town in Dorset, in southern England. Geoffrey says King Hudibras founded it as the town of Mount Paladur, and that an eagle spoke there while its wall was being built.

Wikipedia: [Shaftesbury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shaftesbury)

## Sibyl

Also: Sibyllæ

The Sibyls were prophetesses of the ancient world, whose books of prophecy Rome kept and read in times of danger. Hoel says the Sibyl predicted that three men of British birth would rule the Roman Empire.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Sibyl](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sibyl)

## Sichelm

Also: Sichelini

The Norwegians' king in Geoffrey's story, Lot's uncle, who dies and leaves Lot his throne. The Norwegians refuse Lot and make Riculf king, so Arthur sails to Norway to crown Lot himself.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [King Lot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Lot)

## Silchester

Also: Silcestriam, Silcestriæ, Cilcestriæ

A village in Hampshire, in southern England, beside the ruins of the Roman town of Calleva Atrebatum. In Geoffrey's story the Britons hold their assembly there and crown Constantine king.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Silchester](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silchester)

## Silvius

Also: nomen erat Silvius

Ascanius's son and Brutus's father. In Geoffrey's story he secretly takes a niece of Lavinia as his wife, and soothsayers predict that their son will kill both his parents; Silvius dies by the boy's arrow while hunting.

Wikipedia: [Silvius (mythology)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silvius_(mythology))

## Silvius Epitus

Also: Silvius Epitus, filius Epiti

A king of Alba Longa in Roman legend, Alba Silvius's son, called Atys in the Roman lists of its kings. Geoffrey dates the reigns of Leil and Hudibras by his reign and his son Capys's.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Atys (King of Alba Longa)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atys_(King_of_Alba_Longa))

## Sirens

Also: Sirenes

Sea monsters of Greek myth, part woman and part bird or fish, whose singing drew sailors onto the rocks. Near the Pillars of Hercules they swim round Brutus's ships and nearly sink them.

Wikipedia: [Siren (mythology)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siren_(mythology))

## Sisillius

Also: cui Sisillius, Sisillii filius

A king in Geoffrey's list after Gurgustius. Nothing is told of him but his name and his son Kimarcus, and Wikipedia calls him Sisillius I, since two later kings have the same name.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Sisillius I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sisillius_I)

## Sisillius II

Also: Sisilius, Sisillius sumto

The son of Guithelin and Marcia in Geoffrey's story, seven years old when his father dies, so his mother rules for him. He's crowned when she dies, and his son Kinarius succeeds him. Wikipedia numbers him the second of three kings named Sisillius.

Wikipedia: [Sisillius II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sisillius_II)

## Sisillius III

Also: cui Sisillius

The king after Oenus in Geoffrey's list of the kings of Britain, followed by Blegabred. Geoffrey tells nothing else of him, and Wikipedia numbers him the third of three kings named Sisillius.

Wikipedia: [Sisillius III](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sisillius_III)

## Snowdonia

Also: Erir

The mountains of northwest Wales around Snowdon, Eryri in Welsh. Geoffrey's Vortigern flees there from the Saxons and orders a tower built on Mount Erir, whose walls keep falling.

Wikipedia: [Snowdonia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Snowdonia)

## Soar

Also: Soram, Sora

The river that flows north through Leicester to join the Trent. Geoffrey says King Leir built his city on it, and that Cordelia buried Leir in a chamber under it.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [River Soar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/River_Soar)

## Socrates

Also: Socratis

The Athenian philosopher put to death in 399 BCE, who said a divine voice warned him away from wrong steps. Apuleius wrote a book on that spirit, and Maugantius cites it to Vortigern.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Socrates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Socrates)

## Sodom

Also: Sodomitanæ, Sodomitana

One of the cities the Bible says Yahweh burned with fire and sulfur from the sky. Geoffrey calls Mempricius's lust for men "Sodom's," the sin medieval writers read into the story.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Sodom and Gomorrah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sodom_and_Gomorrah)

## Solomon

Also: Salomon cœpit

David's son and king of Israel, famous for his wisdom, who built the first temple in Jerusalem. Geoffrey dates King Leil's reign by the temple's building and the queen of Sheba's visit to Solomon.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Solomon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solomon)

## Somerset

Also: Sumersetensem

A county of southwest England, between the Bristol Channel and Dorset, with Bath in its northeast corner. In Geoffrey's story Arthur marches into Somerset to break the Saxons' siege of Bath.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Somerset](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Somerset)

## Southampton

Also: Hamtonia

The port city on the south coast of Hampshire. Geoffrey says it's named after Hamo, the Roman commander Arvirargus killed there, and calls it Hamo's Port; its name really comes from the Old English Hamtun.

Wikipedia: [Southampton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southampton)

## Spain

Also: Hispania, Hispaniam, Hispaniæ, Hispaniarum

The Iberian peninsula, today's Spain and Portugal. Geoffrey says the people who first settled Ireland sailed from it, and his history names it again in the wars of Rome.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Spain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spain)

## Sparatinum

Also: Sparatinum

A town in Greece where Brutus leaves a garrison and Pandrasus lays siege. It's known only from Geoffrey's story, and no real town has been found to match it.

Wikipedia: [Pandrasus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pandrasus)

## Sparta

Also: Lacedæmonia

The city in the south of the Greek mainland, Lacedaemon to the ancients, famous for its soldiers. Geoffrey makes Eurystheus its king in the days of Saul.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Sparta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sparta)

## Spring of Galaes

Also: fontem Galaes

A spring Merlin's prophecy names, which the flooding Thames takes to itself before quarrels break out in Gwynedd. Geoffrey doesn't say where it is, and no one has placed it for certain.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## St Davids

Also: Menevia, Meneviam

The small cathedral city at the western tip of Wales, Mynyw in Welsh, where Saint David founded his monastery. Geoffrey first names it as the western end of the road King Belinus builds across the kingdom.

Wikipedia: [St Davids](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St_Davids)

## Staterius

Also: Staterius

A king of Albany in Geoffrey's story, in the years of civil war, who allies with Rudaucus of Wales against Dunvallo Molmutius. He's killed when Dunvallo's men, wearing the enemy's armor, reach him.

Wikipedia: [Staterius](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Staterius)

## Stilbon

Also: Stilbon

Stilbon, "the gleaming one," is the Greeks' name for the planet Mercury, which moves fast and keeps close to the sun. Merlin's prophecy calls it Stilbon of Arcadia, for the land where the god Mercury was born.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Planetae](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Planetae)

## Stonehenge

Also: Stanheng

The great prehistoric ring of standing stones on Salisbury Plain, in Wiltshire. Geoffrey says the English call his Giants' Dance by this name, and buries Aurelius, Uther and Constantine inside it.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Stonehenge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stonehenge)

## Suardus

Also: Suardi

A king of the Franks in Geoffrey's story who helps Ferrex come back from Gaul to fight his brother Porrex for Britain. Nothing else is told of him, and Giles's index calls him Suard.

## Subardus

Also: Subardus

A Poitevin count who turns back from the rout with three hundred men to attack Corineus in the battle in Aquitaine, and is cut in two. He's known only from Geoffrey's story.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Goffar the Pict](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goffar_the_Pict)

## Suesia

Also: Suesia

The valley near Langres in Geoffrey's story where Arthur draws up his army across Lucius Tiberius's road, and where the great battle with the Romans is fought. Neither Giles's index nor San-Marte places it.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## Syria

Also: Syriæ

The land at the east end of the Mediterranean, around Damascus and Antioch, a Roman province in Arthur's day. Geoffrey lists its ruler, Evander, among the eastern kings who come with Lucius against Arthur.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Roman Syria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_Syria)

## Tangustela

Also: Tangustela concubina

Danius's mistress in Geoffrey's story and the mother of his son Morvidus, who becomes king after him. Geoffrey names her only as Morvidus's mother and tells nothing else of her.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Morvidus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morvidus)

## Tenvantius

Also: Tenuantius, Tenuantio, Tenuancius

Lud's younger son in Geoffrey's story, too young to rule when his father dies, so his uncle Cassivellaunus takes the crown and gives him Cornwall to rule as its duke. He's drawn from Tasciovanus, a real British king of the late first century BCE.

Wikipedia: [Tasciovanus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tasciovanus)

## Teucer

Also: Teucer, Teucrum

The duke of Phrygia in Geoffrey's story, one of the rulers of the East who join Lucius Tiberius against Arthur. In the great battle he commands one of the four wedges of the Romans' second line.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## Thadioceus

Also: Thadioceus

The archbishop of York in Geoffrey's story, one of the three archbishops who flee to the woods of Wales with the saints' relics when the Africans and the Saxons pull down the churches. He's known from this one passage.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## Thames

Also: Tamesis, Tamensem, Tamensis

The river of southern England that runs through London to the North Sea, about 215 miles long. Geoffrey names it first of Britain's three great rivers, with the Severn and the Humber, and has Brutus build his city of New Troy on its banks.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [River Thames](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/River_Thames)

## Thanet

Also: Thanet, Tanet

The northeast tip of Kent, then an island cut off by a channel of the sea. Geoffrey's Saxons flee there in their ships when Vortimer beats them, and he besieges them on it.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Isle of Thanet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isle_of_Thanet)

## Theon

Also: Theonus

The bishop of Gloucester in Geoffrey's story, chosen archbishop of London after Arthur's death. When the Africans and the Saxons pull down the churches, he flees with the clergy and the saints' relics to the woods of Wales.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## Thérouanne

Also: Terivana

A small town of northern France, near Saint-Omer, once the seat of a great bishopric. In Geoffrey's story it's the city of Holdinus, ruler of the Ruteni, who's buried there after the great battle.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Thérouanne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Th%C3%A9rouanne)

## Tiber

Also: Tiberim

The river of central Italy that flows about 250 miles from the Apennines through Rome to the Tyrrhenian Sea. Geoffrey says Ascanius built the city of Alba on its banks.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Tiber](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiber)

## Tintagel

Also: Tintagol

A headland fortress on the north coast of Cornwall, cut off from the land by a narrow neck of rock. Geoffrey's Gorlois shuts his wife Igraine up there, out of King Uther's reach.

Wikipedia: [Tintagel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tintagel)

## Totnes

Also: Totonesio, Totonesium, Totonesius

A town on the river Dart in Devon, in southwest England. Geoffrey says Brutus's fleet came ashore on the coast there, the Trojans' first landing in Britain.

Wikipedia: [Totnes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Totnes)

## Tours

Also: Turonorum, Turonis

The city on the Loire in west central France, Caesarodunum to the Romans. Geoffrey says Brutus camped where it now stands, and that it takes its name from his nephew Turonus, who was buried there.

Wikipedia: [Tours](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tours)

## Trahern

Also: Trahern

One of Helena's three uncles in Geoffrey's story, made a senator by Constantine and then sent with three legions to win Britain back from Octavius. Welsh tradition remembers him as Coel's brother, Trahaearn.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Trahern](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trahern)

## Tréguier

Also: Trigeriæ

A port town of northern Brittany, in the Côtes-d'Armor. In Geoffrey's story its earl, Kimarcocus, falls with two thousand men when the Romans surround the Britons of Brittany in the great battle.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Tréguier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tr%C3%A9guier)

## Tremounus

Also: Tremounus

The archbishop of the City of the Legions, Caerleon, in Aurelius's reign in Geoffrey's story. When the king's builders can't think how to honor the murdered lords at Salisbury, he tells Aurelius to send for Merlin. Nothing else is known of him.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## Trier

Also: Treveros

A Roman city on the Moselle river in today's western Germany, one of the capitals of the late empire. In Geoffrey's story Maximianus sets up the throne of his empire there after conquering Gaul and Germany.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Trier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trier)

## Trinovantum

Also: Trinovantum, Trinovanto, Trinovanti, Trojam novam, Trinovantinæ

The name Geoffrey says Brutus's city of New Troy wore for many years, worn down from *Troia Nova*, before King Lud renamed it after himself. The name really belonged to the Trinovantes, a British people of what's now Essex, and Geoffrey's derivation is his own.

Wikipedia: [Trinovantum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trinovantum)

## Trojan War

Also: Trojanum bellum

The legendary ten-year war in which the Greeks besieged and burned Troy, told in Homer's *Iliad* and Virgil's *Aeneid*. Geoffrey's history opens just after it, with Aeneas fleeing the ruined city with his son.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Trojan War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trojan_War)

## Trojans

Also: Trojani, Trojanos, Trojanorum, Troes, Troës, Trojanis

The people of Troy, destroyed by the Greeks in Homer's story. Geoffrey's Brutus is of their royal line, and he leads their descendants out of slavery in Greece to found the Britons.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Troy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Troy)

## Troy

Also: Trojæ, Troja, Trojam

The ancient city in northwest Asia Minor, in today's Turkey, that the Greeks besieged for ten years and burned, in Homer's story. Geoffrey's Britons descend from Trojans who escaped its fall.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Troy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Troy)

## Turnus

Also: Turnus, Turno

The king of the Rutuli in Italy who, in Virgil's *Aeneid*, fought Aeneas for Lavinia, the Latin king's daughter. In Geoffrey's opening lines he grows jealous of Aeneas, fights him and is killed.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Turnus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turnus)

## Turonus

Also: Turonus

Brutus's nephew, the strongest and boldest of the Trojans after Corineus, who kills six hundred men with his own sword before the Gauls kill him. Geoffrey says Tours is named after him, because he was buried there.

Wikipedia: [Brutus of Troy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brutus_of_Troy)

## Tyrrhenian Sea

Also: Tyrrhenum

The part of the Mediterranean between Italy's west coast and the islands of Corsica, Sardinia and Sicily. Geoffrey's Trojans reach it after the Pillars of Hercules and find on its shore four families of exiled Trojans led by Corineus.

Wikipedia: [Tyrrhenian Sea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrrhenian_Sea)

## Ulfin

Also: Ulfin, Ulfinum

Ulfin of Caer Caradog, a friend of King Uther's, who the king tells of his burning love for Igraine and asks for advice. Malory calls him Sir Ulfius, one of Uther's knights.

Wikipedia: [Gorlois](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gorlois)

## Urgennius

Also: Urgennius, Urbgennius

The earl of Bath in Geoffrey's story, one of the earls of the great cities who come to Arthur's crown-wearing in the City of the Legions. Geoffrey tells nothing more of him here.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## Urian

Also: cacumine Uriani

A height Merlin's prophecy names, on whose top the mountain ox is burned and his ashes turn into swans. Geoffrey doesn't say where it is, and no one has placed it for certain.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## Urianus

Also: Urianus Andragii

Andragius's son in Geoffrey's story, who succeeds him as king of Britain. Geoffrey gives nothing but his name and his place in the line, and Eliud follows him.

Wikipedia: [Urianus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Urianus)

## Urien

Also: atque Urianus, fratremque ejus Urianum, Urianus rex Murefensium, Uriani

The brother of Lot and Auguselus in Geoffrey's story, whose family ruled the north before the Saxons came. Arthur gives him the rule of the people of Moray. He's the Urien of Rheged the Welsh poems praise.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Urien Rheged](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Urien_Rheged)

## Ursula

Also: Ursula

The saint of Cologne's legend, who sailed with eleven thousand virgins and was killed with them by the Huns. In Geoffrey's story she's the beautiful daughter of Dionotus, king of Cornwall, and Conan wants her for his wife.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Saint Ursula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint_Ursula)

## Usk

Also: Oscam, Oscæ

The river that runs through south Wales to the Severn estuary at Newport. Geoffrey says Belinus founded a city on it near the Severn sea, the one later called the City of the Legions, Caerleon.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [River Usk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/River_Usk)

## Uther

Also: Uther, Utherpendragon, Utherpendragonem, Uther Pendragon

King Constantine's youngest son, Aurelius Ambrosius's brother, a boy when their father is killed. Geoffrey calls him Utherpendragon, Uther Pendragon, the best known of the kings before Arthur.

Wikipedia: [Uther Pendragon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uther_Pendragon)

## Valentinian

Also: Valentiniani, Valentinianum

Valentinian II, Roman emperor of the west from 375 to 392 CE, Gratian's half-brother. Geoffrey has Maximianus drive him and Gratian from their thrones after they refuse him a third of the empire.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Valentinian II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Valentinian_II)

## Venissa

Also: Genuissa

Claudius's daughter in Geoffrey's story, given to Arvirargus in marriage to seal their peace. She later makes peace between her husband and Vespasian. No such daughter is known, and Giles prints her name Genuissa.

Wikipedia: [Venissa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Venissa)

## Venus

Also: vocabit Venerem, Venerei, castra Veneris, Venus

The Roman goddess of love and beauty, the mother of Aeneas and of Cupid, and the bright planet named for her. Merlin's prophecy names a goat of her castle and her camps of love, and later her planet among the stars.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Venus (mythology)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Venus_(mythology))

## Verulamium

Also: Verolamium, Verolamio, Verolamius

The Roman town on the Ver, beside today's St Albans, in Hertfordshire, one of the largest towns of Roman Britain. Geoffrey's Uther, sick and carried on a stretcher, besieges the Saxons there.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Verulamium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Verulamium)

## Vespasian

Also: Vespasianus

The Roman general who conquered the southwest of Britain under Claudius in 43 CE and became emperor in 69 CE. Geoffrey has him sent against Arvirargus, fight him at Exeter, and go home at peace.

Wikipedia: [Vespasian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vespasian)

## Virgo

Also: Virgo

The virgin, the sixth sign of the zodiac, drawn as a young woman, which the sun passes through at the end of summer. In Merlin's prophecy she climbs on the back of Sagittarius, the archer.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Virgo (astrology)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Virgo_(astrology))

## Vortigern

Also: Vortegirnus, Vortegirno, Vortegirnum, Vortegirni

A lord of the Gewissae, the most powerful man among the Britons after King Constantine's death, who schemes his way toward the throne through the young monk-king Constans. He's the king British legend blames for bringing the Saxons into Britain.

Wikipedia: [Vortigern](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vortigern)

## Vortimer

Also: Vortimer, Vortimerius, Vortimerium, Vortimerii

Vortigern's oldest son, named with his brothers Catigern and Pascentius. British legend remembered him as a hero who fought the Saxons after his father gave in to them.

Wikipedia: [Vortimer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vortimer)

## Vortiporius

Also: Wortiporius

A king of Dyfed, in southwest Wales, in the 500s CE, one of the kings Gildas condemned. Geoffrey makes him king of all Britain and says he beat the Saxons when they rose against him.

Wikipedia: [Vortiporius](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vortiporius)

## Vulteius Catellus

Also: Vulteium Catellum, Vultei Catello

A Roman senator in Geoffrey's story who leads the ambush on the Britons taking the prisoners to Paris. He's killed when Guitardus comes up with help and the Britons turn the fight.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## Walbrook

Also: Nautgallim, Gallemborne

A stream that ran through Roman London into the Thames and now flows under the City's streets. Geoffrey says it took its name from the Roman Livius Gallus, killed beside it, but the name more likely meant the Britons' stream or the stream by the wall.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [River Walbrook](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/River_Walbrook)

## Wales

Also: Guallia, Gualias, Guallias, Gualliis, Gualiis, Gualliarum, Kambria, Cambria, Cambriam, Cambriæ, Kambriæ

The country west of the Severn, the land of the Welsh. Geoffrey says it was Kamber's share of Brutus's kingdom, called Kambria after him, and that its people still call themselves Kambri, Cymry in Welsh.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Wales](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wales)

## Walter of Oxford

Also: Walterus Oxinefordensis, Gualtero Oxinefordensi, Gualterus Oxinefordensis

Walter, archdeacon of Oxford in the 1100s CE, a learned man and a friend of Geoffrey's. Geoffrey says Walter gave him a very old book in the British tongue running from Brutus to Cadwaladr, which he translated into Latin. No such book has ever been found.

Wikipedia: [Walter of Oxford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walter_of_Oxford)

## Wanius

Also: Guanius, Guanii

King of the Huns in Geoffrey's story, who with Melga, king of the Picts, raids the coasts of Germany for Gratian and then invades Britain once its soldiers have gone. Giles prints him Guanius, and he's known only from Geoffrey.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Dionotus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dionotus)

## Westmorland

Also: Westimaria, Westmarialanda

A county of northwest England, now part of Cumbria. Geoffrey says it's named after Marius, who set up a stone there for his victory over Rodric, but its name means the land of the people west of the moors.

Wikipedia: [Westmorland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Westmorland)

## William of Malmesbury

Also: Guillelmo Malmesberiensi

A monk of Malmesbury Abbey and the leading English historian of the early 1100s CE, who wrote a history of the English kings. Geoffrey leaves the Saxon kings to him, and tells him to say nothing of the British ones.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [William of Malmesbury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_of_Malmesbury)

## Winchester

Also: Guintoniam, Guintonia, Guintoniæ, Kaerguen, Wintoniam

The city in Hampshire, in southern England, the old capital of the English kings, Venta Belgarum to the Romans. Geoffrey says King Hudibras built it and called it Kaerguen.

Wikipedia: [Winchester](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Winchester)

## Winwaed

Also: Winved

A river near Leeds where in 655 CE Oswiu of Northumbria beat and killed Penda of Mercia. Geoffrey tells the battle, saying Penda died there with thirty of his chief men.

Wikipedia: [Battle of the Winwaed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_the_Winwaed)

## Woden

Also: Woden

The chief god of the pagan English, Odin to the Norse, who Wednesday is named after. Hengist tells Vortigern that the Saxons worship him above all, and that he's the god the Romans call Mercury.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Odin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Odin)

## Worcester

Also: Wigorniæ, Guigornensis, Wigornensium

A cathedral city on the Severn in Worcestershire, in the west of England, about thirty miles north of Gloucester. Merlin's prophecy names a dragon of Worcester that a giant rides.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Worcester, England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Worcester,_England)

## Wulfhere

Also: Wulfredus

The son of Penda, and king of Mercia from 658 CE, who won his father's kingdom back from Oswiu. In Geoffrey's story Cadwallon gives him the kingdom, and he rebels against Oswiu until Cadwallon orders peace.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Wulfhere of Mercia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wulfhere_of_Mercia)

## Wye

Also: Ganiæ

The river that rises in the mountains of mid Wales and runs through Herefordshire to the Severn at Chepstow, much of its way along the border of England and Wales. Geoffrey sets Vortigern's last fort above it.

Wikipedia: [River Wye](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/River_Wye)

## Yahweh

The god Geoffrey's Christians serve, which his Latin calls *Deus*, named Yahweh in this translation by its rule on the god's name. Geoffrey says Yahweh punished the Britons' pride by letting the Picts and Saxons drive them out.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Yahweh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yahweh)

## York

Also: Eboracum, Eboraci, Eboraco, Kaerebrauc, Eboracensis

The city on the Ouse in northern England, Eboracum to the Romans. Geoffrey says King Ebraucus built it and called it Kaerebrauc, the city of Ebrauc, after himself.

Wikipedia: [York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/York)

## Æthelstan

Also: Athelstano

King of the English from 924 to 939 CE, Alfred the Great's grandson, the first to rule all England, who made the Welsh kings pay him tribute. The Welsh annals record his death.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Æthelstan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C3%86thelstan)
